                ssh-mldsa44-ed25519-cert,
                ssh-ed25519,
                ecdsa-sha2-nistp256,ecdsa-sha2-nistp384,ecdsa-sha2-nistp521,
                sk-ssh-ed25519@openssh.com,
                sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com,
                webauthn-sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com,
                rsa-sha2-512,rsa-sha2-256,
                ssh-mldsa44-ed25519

             The list of  available  signature  algorithms  may  also  be  obtained  using  "ssh  -Q
             PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms".

     1mPubkeyAuthentication0m
             Specifies  whether to try public key authentication.  The argument to this keyword must
             be 1myes 22m(the default), 1mno22m, 1munbound 22mor 1mhost-bound22m.  The final two options  enable  public
             key  authentication while respectively disabling or enabling the OpenSSH host-bound au‐
             thentication protocol extension required for restricted 8;;man:ssh-agent(1)4mssh-agent24m(1)8;; forwarding.

     1mRefuseConnection0m
             Allows a connection to be refused by the configuration file.  If this option is  speci‐
             fied, then 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;; will terminate immediately before attempting to connect to the remote
             host,  display an error message that contains the argument to this keyword and return a
             non-zero exit status.  This option may be useful to express reminders  or  warnings  to
             the user via 1mssh_config22m.

     1mRekeyLimit0m
             Specifies  the  maximum  amount  of data that may be transmitted or received before the
             session key is renegotiated, optionally followed by a maximum amount of time  that  may
             pass  before the session key is renegotiated.  The first argument is specified in bytes
             and may have a suffix of ‘K’, ‘M’, or ‘G’ to indicate Kilobytes,  Megabytes,  or  Giga‐
             bytes,  respectively.   The  default is between ‘1G’ and ‘4G’, depending on the cipher.
             The optional second value is specified in seconds and may use any of  the  units  docu‐
             mented in the TIME FORMATS section of 8;;man:sshd_config(5)4msshd_config24m(5)8;;.  The default value for 1mRekeyLimit0m
             is  1mdefault  none22m,  which  means  that rekeying is performed after the cipher's default
             amount of data has been sent or received and no time based rekeying is done.

     1mRemoteCommand0m
             Specifies a command to execute on the remote machine after successfully  connecting  to
             the  server.   The  command string extends to the end of the line, and is executed with
             the user's shell.  Arguments to  1mRemoteCommand  22maccept  the  tokens  described  in  the
             “TOKENS” section.

     1mRemoteForward0m
             Specifies that a TCP port or Unix-domain socket on the remote machine be forwarded over
             the  secure  channel.   The remote port may either be forwarded to a specified host and
             port or Unix-domain socket from the local machine, or may act as a SOCKS 4/5 proxy that
             allows a remote client to connect to arbitrary destinations  from  the  local  machine.
             The first argument is the listening specification and may be [4mbind_address24m:]4mport24m or, if
             the  remote  host  supports it, a Unix domain socket path.  If forwarding to a specific
             destination then the second argument must be 4mhost24m:4mhostport24m  or  a  Unix  domain  socket
             path, otherwise if no destination argument is specified then the remote forwarding will
             be  established as a SOCKS proxy.  When acting as a SOCKS proxy, the destination of the
             connection can be restricted by 1mPermitRemoteOpen22m.

             IPv6 addresses can be specified by enclosing addresses in square brackets.

             If either argument contains a '/' in it, that argument will be interpreted as  a  Unix-
             domain socket (on the corresponding host) rather than a TCP port.

             Multiple  forwardings  may be specified, and additional forwardings can be given on the
             command line.  Privileged ports can be forwarded only when logging in as  root  on  the
             remote  machine.  Unix domain socket paths may use the tokens described in the “TOKENS”
             section and environment variables as described in the “ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES” section.

             If the 4mport24m argument is 0, the listen port will be dynamically allocated on the  server
             and reported to the client at run time.

             If  the  4mbind_address24m  is  not  specified,  the default is to only bind to loopback ad‐
             dresses.  If the 4mbind_address24m is ‘*’ or an empty string, then  the  forwarding  is  re‐
             quested  to  listen on all interfaces.  Specifying a remote 4mbind_address24m will only suc‐
             ceed if the server's 1mGatewayPorts 22moption is enabled (see 8;;man:sshd_config(5)4msshd_config24m(5)8;;).

     1mRequestTTY0m
             Specifies whether to request a pseudo-tty for the session.  The argument may be one of:
             1mno 22m(never request a TTY), 1myes 22m(always request a TTY when  standard  input  is  a  TTY),
             1mforce  22m(always  request  a  TTY)  or 1mauto 22m(request a TTY when opening a login session).
             This option mirrors the 1m-t 22mand 1m-T 22mflags for 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;;.

     1mRequiredRSASize0m
             Specifies the minimum RSA key size (in bits) that 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;; will accept.  User authentica‐
             tion keys smaller than this limit will be ignored.   Servers  that  present  host  keys
             smaller  than  this  limit  will cause the connection to be terminated.  The default is
             1m1024 22mbits.  Note that this limit may only be raised from the default.

     1mRevokedHostKeys0m
             Specifies revoked host public keys.  Keys listed in this file will be refused for  host
             authentication.   Note  that  if this file does not exist or is not readable, then host
             authentication will be refused for all hosts.  Keys may be specified as  a  text  file,
             listing  one  public key per line, or as an OpenSSH Key Revocation List (KRL) as gener‐
             ated by 8;;man:ssh-keygen(1)4mssh-keygen24m(1)8;;.  For more information on KRLs, see the KEY REVOCATION LISTS sec‐
             tion in 8;;man:ssh-keygen(1)4mssh-keygen24m(1)8;;.  Arguments to 1mRevokedHostKeys 22mmay use the tilde syntax to  refer
             to  a  user's home directory, the tokens described in the “TOKENS” section and environ‐
             ment variables as described in the “ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES” section.

     1mSecurityKeyProvider0m
             Specifies a path to a library that will be used when loading  any  FIDO  authenticator-
             hosted keys, overriding the default of using the built-in USB HID support.

             If the specified value begins with a ‘$’ character, then it will be treated as an envi‐
             ronment variable containing the path to the library.

     1mSendEnv0m
             Specifies  what  variables from the local 8;;man:environ(7)4menviron24m(7)8;; should be sent to the server.  The
             server must also support it, and the server must be configured to accept these environ‐
             ment variables.  Note that the 4mTERM24m environment variable  is  always  sent  whenever  a
             pseudo-terminal  is requested as it is required by the protocol.  Refer to 1mAcceptEnv 22min
             8;;man:sshd_config(5)4msshd_config24m(5)8;; for how to configure the server.  Variables are specified by name, which
             may contain wildcard characters.  Multiple environment variables may  be  separated  by
             whitespace or spread across multiple 1mSendEnv 22mdirectives.

             See “PATTERNS” for more information on patterns.

             It  is  possible  to  clear previously set 1mSendEnv 22mvariable names by prefixing patterns
             with 4m-24m.  The default is not to send any environment variables.

     1mServerAliveCountMax0m
             Sets the number of server alive messages (see below) which may be sent  without  8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;;
             receiving any messages back from the server.  If this threshold is reached while server
             alive  messages  are  being  sent, ssh will disconnect from the server, terminating the
             session.  It is important to note that the use of server alive messages is very differ‐
             ent from 1mTCPKeepAlive 22m(below).  The server alive messages  are  sent  through  the  en‐
             crypted  channel and therefore will not be spoofable.  The TCP keepalive option enabled
             by 1mTCPKeepAlive 22mis spoofable.  The server alive mechanism is valuable when  the  client
             or server depend on knowing when a connection has become unresponsive.

             The  default value is 3.  If, for example, 1mServerAliveInterval 22m(see below) is set to 15
             and 1mServerAliveCountMax 22mis left at the default, if the server becomes unresponsive, ssh
             will disconnect after approximately 45 seconds.

     1mServerAliveInterval0m
             Sets a timeout interval in seconds after which if no data has been  received  from  the
             server,  8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;; will send a message through the encrypted channel to request a response
             from the server.  The default is 0, indicating that these messages will not be sent  to
             the server.

     1mSessionType0m
             May  be  used  to  either request invocation of a subsystem on the remote system, or to
             prevent the execution of a remote command at all.  The latter is useful for  just  for‐
             warding  ports.   The  argument  to  this keyword must be 1mnone 22m(same as the 1m-N 22moption),
             1msubsystem 22m(same as the 1m-s 22moption) or 1mdefault 22m(shell or command execution).

     1mSetEnv  22mDirectly specify one or more environment variables and their contents to be sent to the
             server in the form “NAME=VALUE”.  Similarly to 1mSendEnv22m, with the exception of the  4mTERM0m
             variable, the server must be prepared to accept the environment variable.

             The  “VALUE” may use the tokens described in the “TOKENS” section and environment vari‐
             ables as described in the “ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES” section.

     1mStdinNull0m
             Redirects stdin from 4m/dev/null24m (actually, prevents reading from stdin).  Either this or
             the equivalent 1m-n 22moption must be used when 1mssh 22mis run in the background.  The  argument
             to this keyword must be 1myes 22m(same as the 1m-n 22moption) or 1mno 22m(the default).

     1mStreamLocalBindMask0m
             Sets  the octal file creation mode mask (umask) used when creating a Unix-domain socket
             file for local or remote port forwarding.  This option is only used for port forwarding
             to a Unix-domain socket file.

             The default value is 0177, which creates a Unix-domain socket file that is readable and
             writable only by the owner.  Note that not all operating systems honor the file mode on
             Unix-domain socket files.

     1mStreamLocalBindUnlink0m
             Specifies whether to remove an existing Unix-domain socket file  for  local  or  remote
             port  forwarding  before  creating  a  new  one.  If the socket file already exists and
             1mStreamLocalBindUnlink 22mis not enabled, 1mssh 22mwill be unable to forward  the  port  to  the
             Unix-domain socket file.  This option is only used for port forwarding to a Unix-domain
             socket file.

             The argument must be 1myes 22mor 1mno 22m(the default).

     1mStrictHostKeyChecking0m
             If  this  flag  is  set  to  1myes22m,  8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;; will never automatically add host keys to the
             4m~/.ssh/known_hosts24m file, and refuses to connect to hosts whose host  key  has  changed.
             This  provides  maximum  protection against man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks, though it
             can be annoying when the 4m/etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts24m file is  poorly  maintained  or  when
             connections  to new hosts are frequently made.  This option forces the user to manually
             add all new hosts.

             If this flag is set to 1maccept-new 22mthen ssh will automatically add new host keys to  the
             user's  4mknown_hosts24m  file,  but  will not permit connections to hosts with changed host
             keys.  If this flag is set to 1mno 22mor 1moff22m, ssh will automatically add new  host  keys  to
             the user known hosts files and allow connections to hosts with changed hostkeys to pro‐
             ceed, subject to some restrictions.  If this flag is set to 1mask 22m(the default), new host
             keys  will be added to the user known host files only after the user has confirmed that
             is what they really want to do, and ssh will refuse to connect to hosts whose host  key
             has changed.  The host keys of known hosts will be verified automatically in all cases.

     1mSyslogFacility0m
             Gives  the  facility code that is used when logging messages from 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;;.  The possible
             values are: DAEMON, USER, AUTH, LOCAL0, LOCAL1, LOCAL2, LOCAL3, LOCAL4, LOCAL5, LOCAL6,
             LOCAL7.  The default is USER.

     1mTCPKeepAlive0m
             Specifies whether the system should send keepalive  messages  on  TCP  sockets  it  has
             opened.   If  they are sent, failure of the connection or crash of one of the endpoints
             may be more promptly detected.  However, this means that connections may  terminate  if
             the connection is suffers a transient disruption.

             The  argument  must  be 1mtransport 22mto enable TCP keepalive messages on the SSH transport
             connection to the server, 1myes 22mwhich is an  alias  for  1mtransport22m,  1mall  22mto  enable  TCP
             keepalive  messages  on all sockets opened by 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;;, including sockets created for X11
             or port forwarding, or 1mno 22mto disable TCP keepalive messages.  The default is 1mtransport22m.

             See also 1mServerAliveInterval 22mfor a more robust connection failure  detection  mechanism
             that works at the SSH protocol level.

     1mTag     22mSpecify  a configuration tag name that may be later used by a 1mMatch 22mdirective to select
             a block of configuration.

     1mTunnel  22mRequest 8;;man:tun(4)4mtun24m(4)8;; device forwarding between the client and the server.  The argument  must
             be  1myes22m, 1mpoint-to-point 22m(layer 3), 1methernet 22m(layer 2), or 1mno 22m(the default).  Specifying
             1myes 22mrequests the default tunnel mode, which is 1mpoint-to-point22m.

     1mTunnelDevice0m
             Specifies the 8;;man:tun(4)4mtun24m(4)8;;  devices  to  open  on  the  client  (4mlocal_tun24m)  and  the  server
             (4mremote_tun24m).

             The argument must be 4mlocal_tun24m[:4mremote_tun24m].  The devices may be specified by numerical
             ID  or  the keyword 1many22m, which uses the next available tunnel device.  If 4mremote_tun24m is
             not specified, it defaults to 1many22m.  The default is 1many:any22m.

     1mUpdateHostKeys0m
             Specifies whether 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;; should accept notifications of additional  hostkeys  from  the
             server sent after authentication has completed and add them to 1mUserKnownHostsFile22m.  The
             argument  must be 1myes22m, 1mno 22mor 1mask22m.  This option allows learning alternate hostkeys for a
             server and supports graceful key rotation by allowing a server to send replacement pub‐
             lic keys before old ones are removed.

             Additional hostkeys are only accepted if the key used to authenticate the host was  al‐
             ready  trusted  or  explicitly  accepted  by  the  user, the host was authenticated via
             1mUserKnownHostsFile 22m(i.e. not 1mGlobalKnownHostsFile22m) and the host was authenticated using
             a plain key and not a certificate.

             1mUpdateHostKeys 22mis enabled by default  if  the  user  has  not  overridden  the  default
             1mUserKnownHostsFile   22msetting   and   has   not   enabled   1mVerifyHostKeyDNS22m,  otherwise
             1mUpdateHostKeys 22mwill be set to 1mno22m.

             If 1mUpdateHostKeys 22mis set to 1mask22m, then the user is asked to confirm the modifications to
             the known_hosts file.  Confirmation is currently incompatible with 1mControlPersist22m,  and
             will be disabled if it is enabled.

             Presently, only 8;;man:sshd(8)4msshd24m(8)8;; from OpenSSH 6.8 and greater support the "hostkeys@openssh.com"
             protocol extension used to inform the client of all the server's hostkeys.

     1mUser    22mSpecifies the user to log in as.  This can be useful when a different user name is used
             on  different  machines.  This saves the trouble of having to remember to give the user
             name on the command line.  Arguments to 1mUser  22mmay  use  the  tokens  described  in  the
             “TOKENS”  section  (with  the  exception of %r and %C) and environment variables as de‐
             scribed in the “ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES” section.

     1mUserKnownHostsFile0m
             Specifies one or more files to use for the user host key database, separated by  white‐
             space.  Each filename may use tilde notation to refer to the user's home directory, the
             tokens  described in the “TOKENS” section and environment variables as described in the
             “ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES” section.  A value of 1mnone 22mcauses 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;; to ignore any user-spe‐
             cific known hosts files.  The default is 4m~/.ssh/known_hosts24m, 4m~/.ssh/known_hosts224m.

     1mVerifyHostKeyDNS0m
             Specifies whether to verify the remote key using DNS and SSHFP  resource  records.   If
             this  option  is  set to 1myes22m, the client will implicitly trust keys that match a secure
             fingerprint from DNS.  Insecure fingerprints will be handled as if this option was  set
             to  1mask22m.   If  this option is set to 1mask22m, information on fingerprint match will be dis‐
             played, but the user will still  need  to  confirm  new  host  keys  according  to  the
             1mStrictHostKeyChecking 22moption.  The default is 1mno22m.

             See also “VERIFYING HOST KEYS” in 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;;.

     1mVersionAddendum0m
             Optionally  specifies  additional text to append to the SSH protocol banner sent by the
             client upon connection.  The default is 1mnone22m.

     1mVisualHostKey0m
             If this flag is set to 1myes22m, an ASCII art representation of the remote host key  finger‐
             print  is  printed  in addition to the fingerprint string at login and for unknown host
             keys.  If this flag is set to 1mno 22m(the default), no fingerprint strings are  printed  at
             login and only the fingerprint string will be printed for unknown host keys.

     1mWarnWeakCrypto0m
             controls  whether  the  user is warned when the cryptographic algorithms negotiated for
             the connection are weak or otherwise recommended against.  Warnings may be disabled  by
             turning  off  a  specific warning or by disabling all warnings.  Warnings about connec‐
             tions that don't use a post-quantum key exchange may be disabled  using  the  1mno-pq-kex0m
             flag.   1mno 22mwill disable all warnings.  The default, equivalent to 1myes22m, is to enable all
             warnings.

     1mXAuthLocation0m
             Specifies the full pathname of the 8;;man:xauth(1)4mxauth24m(1)8;; program.  The default is 4m/usr/bin/xauth24m.

1mPATTERNS0m
     A 4mpattern24m consists of zero or more non-whitespace characters, ‘*’ (a wildcard that matches zero
     or more characters), or ‘?’ (a wildcard that matches exactly one character).  For  example,  to
     specify  a  set of declarations for any host in the ".co.uk" set of domains, the following pat‐
     tern could be used:

           1mHost *.co.uk0m

     The following pattern would match any host in the 192.168.0.[0-9] network range:

           1mHost 192.168.0.?0m

     A 4mpattern-list24m is a comma-separated list of patterns.  Patterns  within  pattern-lists  may  be
     negated  by  preceding  them with an exclamation mark (‘!’).  For example, to allow a key to be
     used from anywhere within an organization except from the "dialup" pool,  the  following  entry
     (in authorized_keys) could be used:

           1mfrom="!*.dialup.example.com,*.example.com"0m

     Note  that  a  negated  match will never produce a positive result by itself.  For example, at‐
     tempting to match "host3" against the following pattern-list will fail:

           1mfrom="!host1,!host2"0m

     The solution here is to include a term that will yield a positive match, such as a wildcard:

           1mfrom="!host1,!host2,*"0m

1mTOKENS0m
     Arguments to some keywords can make use of tokens, which are expanded at runtime.   Tokens  are
     expanded  without  quoting or escaping of shell characters.  It is the user's responsibility to
     ensure they are safe in the context of their use.

     The supported tokens in 1mssh_config 22mare:

           %%    A literal ‘%’.
           %C    Hash of %l%h%p%r%j.
           %d    Local user's home directory.
           %f    The fingerprint of the server's host key.
           %H    The 4mknown_hosts24m hostname or address that is being searched for.
           %h    The remote hostname.
           %I    A string describing the reason for a 1mKnownHostsCommand  22mexecution:  either  1mADDRESS0m
                 when looking up a host by address (only when 1mCheckHostIP 22mis enabled), 1mHOSTNAME 22mwhen
                 searching  by  hostname,  or 1mORDER 22mwhen preparing the host key algorithm preference
                 list to use for the destination host.
           %i    The local user ID.
           %j    The contents of the ProxyJump option, or the empty string if this option is unset.
           %K    The base64 encoded host key.
           %k    The host key alias if specified, otherwise the original remote  hostname  given  on
                 the command line.
           %L    The local hostname.
           %l    The local hostname, including the domain name.
           %n    The original remote hostname, as given on the command line.
           %p    The remote port.
           %r    The remote username.
           %T    The  local 8;;man:tun(4)4mtun24m(4)8;; or 8;;man:tap(4)4mtap24m(4)8;; network interface assigned if tunnel forwarding was re‐
                 quested, or "NONE" otherwise.
           %t    The type of the server host key, e.g.  1mssh-ed2551922m.
           %u    The local username.

     1mCertificateFile22m,  1mControlPath22m,   1mIdentityAgent22m,   1mIdentityFile22m,   1mInclude22m,   1mKnownHostsCommand22m,
     1mLocalForward22m, 1mMatch exec22m, 1mRemoteCommand22m, 1mRemoteForward22m, 1mRevokedHostKeys22m, 1mUserKnownHostsFile 22mand
     1mVersionAddendum 22maccept the tokens %%, %C, %d, %h, %i, %j, %k, %L, %l, %n, %p, %r, and %u.

     1mKnownHostsCommand 22madditionally accepts the tokens %f, %H, %I, %K and %t.

     1mHostname 22maccepts the tokens %% and %h.

     1mLocalCommand 22maccepts all tokens.

     1mProxyCommand 22mand 1mProxyJump 22maccept the tokens %%, %h, %n, %p, and %r.

     Note  that some of these directives build commands for execution via the shell.  Because 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;;
     performs no filtering or escaping of characters that have special  meaning  in  shell  commands
     (e.g. quotes), it is the user's responsibility to ensure that the arguments passed to 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;; do
     not contain such characters and that tokens are appropriately quoted when used.

1mENVIRONMENT VARIABLES0m
     Arguments  to some keywords can be expanded at runtime from environment variables on the client
     by enclosing them in 1m${}22m, for example 1m${HOME}/.ssh 22mwould refer to the  user's  .ssh  directory.
     If  a specified environment variable does not exist then an error will be returned and the set‐
     ting for that keyword will be ignored.

     The   keywords   1mCertificateFile22m,   1mControlPath22m,    1mIdentityAgent22m,    1mIdentityFile22m,    1mInclude22m,
     1mKnownHostsCommand22m,   and   1mUserKnownHostsFile  22msupport  environment  variables.   The  keywords
     1mLocalForward 22mand 1mRemoteForward 22msupport environment variables only for Unix domain socket paths.

1mFILES0m
     4m~/.ssh/config0m
             This is the per-user configuration file.  The format of this file is  described  above.
             This  file  is  used  by the SSH client.  Because of the potential for abuse, this file
             must have strict permissions: read/write for the user, and not writable by others.

     4m/etc/ssh/ssh_config0m
             Systemwide configuration file.  This file provides defaults for those values  that  are
             not  specified  in the user's configuration file, and for those users who do not have a
             configuration file.  This file must be world-readable.

1mSEE ALSO0m
     8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;;

sshd.text:
4mSSHD24m(8)                                System Manager's Manual                               4mSSHD24m(8)

1mNAME0m
     1msshd 22m—— OpenSSH daemon

1mSYNOPSIS0m
     1msshd 22m[1m-46DdeGiqTtV22m] [1m-C 4m22mconnection_spec24m] [1m-c 4m22mhost_certificate_file24m] [1m-E 4m22mlog_file24m]
          [1m-f 4m22mconfig_file24m] [1m-g 4m22mlogin_grace_time24m] [1m-h 4m22mhost_key_file24m] [1m-o 4m22moption24m] [1m-p 4m22mport24m] [1m-u 4m22mlen24m]

1mDESCRIPTION0m
     1msshd  22m(OpenSSH Daemon) is the daemon program for 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;;.  It provides secure encrypted communi‐
     cations between two untrusted hosts over an insecure network.

     1msshd 22mlistens for connections from clients.  It is normally started at boot  from  4m/etc/rc24m.   It
     forks  a  new daemon for each incoming connection.  The forked daemons handle key exchange, en‐
     cryption, authentication, command execution, and data exchange.

     1msshd 22mcan be configured using command-line options or a configuration file (by default 8;;man:sshd_config(5)4msshd_con‐0m
     4mfig24m(5)8;;); command-line options override  values  specified  in  the  configuration  file.   1msshd0m
     rereads  its  configuration  file when it receives a hangup signal, SIGHUP, by executing itself
     with the name and options it was started with, e.g. 4m/usr/sbin/sshd24m.

     The options are as follows:

     1m-4      22mForces 1msshd 22mto use IPv4 addresses only.

     1m-6      22mForces 1msshd 22mto use IPv6 addresses only.

1mAUTHENTICATION0m
     The OpenSSH SSH daemon supports SSH protocol 2 only.  Each host has a host-specific  key,  used
     to  identify  the  host.   Whenever a client connects, the daemon responds with its public host
     key.  The client compares the host key against its own database  to  verify  that  it  has  not
     changed.   Forward secrecy is provided through a Diffie-Hellman key agreement.  This key agree‐
     ment results in a shared session key.  The rest of the session is encrypted using  a  symmetric
     cipher.   The  client selects the encryption algorithm to use from those offered by the server.
     Additionally, session integrity is provided through a cryptographic message authentication code
     (MAC).

     Finally, the server and the client enter an authentication dialog.  The client tries to authen‐
     ticate itself using host-based authentication, public  key  authentication,  challenge-response
     authentication, or password authentication.

     Regardless  of the authentication type, the account is checked to ensure that it is accessible.
     An account is not accessible if it is locked, listed in 1mDenyUsers 22mor its  group  is  listed  in
     1mDenyGroups 22m.  The definition of a locked account is system dependent. Some platforms have their
     own  account  database  (eg  AIX)  and  some  modify  the  passwd field ( ‘*LK*’ on Solaris and
     UnixWare, ‘*’ on HP-UX, containing ‘Nologin’ on Tru64, a leading ‘*LOCKED*’ on  FreeBSD  and  a
     leading ‘!’ on most Linuxes).  If there is a requirement to disable password authentication for
     the  account  while allowing still public-key, then the passwd field should be set to something
     other than these values (eg ‘NP’ or ‘*NP*’ ).

     If the client successfully authenticates itself, a dialog for preparing the session is entered.
     At this time the client may request things like allocating a pseudo-tty, forwarding X11 connec‐
     tions, forwarding TCP connections, or forwarding the authentication agent connection  over  the
     secure channel.

     After  this,  the client either requests an interactive shell or execution of a non-interactive
     command, which 1msshd 22mwill execute via the user's shell using its 1m-c 22moption.  The sides then  en‐
     ter  session  mode.  In this mode, either side may send data at any time, and such data is for‐
     warded to/from the shell or command on the server side, and the user  terminal  in  the  client
     side.

     When  the user program terminates and all forwarded X11 and other connections have been closed,
     the server sends command exit status to the client, and both sides exit.

1mLOGIN PROCESS0m
     When a user successfully logs in, 1msshd 22mdoes the following:

           1.   If the login is on a tty, and no command has been specified, prints last login  time
                and  4m/etc/motd24m  (unless  prevented in the configuration file or by 4m~/.hushlogin24m; see
                the “FILES” section).

           2.   If the login is on a tty, records login time.

           3.   Checks 4m/etc/nologin24m; if it exists, prints contents and quits (unless root).

           4.   Changes to run with normal user privileges.

           5.   Sets up basic environment.

           6.   Reads the file 4m~/.ssh/environment24m, if it exists, and users  are  allowed  to  change
                their environment.  See the 1mPermitUserEnvironment 22moption in 8;;man:sshd_config(5)4msshd_config24m(5)8;;.

           7.   Changes to user's home directory.

           8.   If 4m~/.ssh/rc24m exists and the 8;;man:sshd_config(5)4msshd_config24m(5)8;; 1mPermitUserRC 22moption is set, runs it; else
                if  4m/etc/ssh/sshrc24m  exists,  runs  it;  otherwise runs 8;;man:xauth(1)4mxauth24m(1)8;;.  The “rc” files are
                given the X11 authentication protocol and cookie in standard  input.   See  “SSHRC”,
                below.

           9.   Runs  user's shell or command.  All commands are run under the user's login shell as
                specified in the system password database.

1mSSHRC0m
     If the file 4m~/.ssh/rc24m exists, 8;;man:sh(1)4msh24m(1)8;; runs it after reading  the  environment  files  but  before
     starting the user's shell or command.  It must not produce any output on stdout; stderr must be
     used  instead.   If  X11  forwarding  is in use, it will receive the "proto cookie" pair in its
     standard input (and 4mDISPLAY24m in its environment).  The script must call  8;;man:xauth(1)4mxauth24m(1)8;;  because  1msshd0m
     will not run xauth automatically to add X11 cookies.

     The  primary purpose of this file is to run any initialization routines which may be needed be‐
     fore the user's home directory becomes accessible; AFS is a particular example of such an envi‐
     ronment.

     This file will probably contain some initialization code followed by something similar to:

        if read proto cookie && [ -n "$DISPLAY" ]; then
                if [ ‘echo $DISPLAY | cut -c1-10‘ = 'localhost:' ]; then
                        # X11UseLocalhost=yes
                        echo add unix:‘echo $DISPLAY |
                            cut -c11-‘ $proto $cookie
                else
                        # X11UseLocalhost=no
                        echo add $DISPLAY $proto $cookie
                fi | xauth -q -
        fi

     If this file does not exist, 4m/etc/ssh/sshrc24m is run, and if that does not exist either, xauth is
     used to add the cookie.

1mAUTHORIZED_KEYS FILE FORMAT0m
     1mAuthorizedKeysFile 22mspecifies the files containing public keys for public key authentication; if
     this   option   is   not    specified,    the    default    is    4m~/.ssh/authorized_keys24m    and
     4m~/.ssh/authorized_keys224m.   Each line of the file contains one key (empty lines and lines start‐
     ing with a ‘#’ are ignored as comments).  Public keys consist of the following  space-separated
     fields:  options,  keytype,  base64-encoded  key, comment.  The options field is optional.  The
     supported key types are:

           sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com
           ecdsa-sha2-nistp256
           ecdsa-sha2-nistp384
           ecdsa-sha2-nistp521
           sk-ssh-ed25519@openssh.com
           ssh-ed25519
           ssh-mldsa44-ed25519
           ssh-rsa

     The comment field is not used for anything (but may be convenient for the user to identify  the
     key).

     Note that lines in this file can be several hundred bytes long (because of the size of the pub‐
     lic  key encoding) up to a limit of 8 kilobytes, which permits RSA keys up to 16 kilobits.  You
     don't want to type them in; instead, copy the  4mid_ecdsa.pub24m,  4mid_ecdsa_sk.pub24m,  4mid_ed25519.pub24m,
     4mid_ed25519_sk.pub24m, 4mid_mldsa44_ed25519.pub24m, or the 4mid_rsa.pub24m file and edit it.

     1msshd 22menforces a minimum RSA key modulus size of 1024 bits.

     The  options (if present) consist of comma-separated option specifications.  No spaces are per‐
     mitted, except within double quotes.  The following option specifications are  supported  (note
     that option keywords are case-insensitive):

     1magent-forwarding0m
             Enable authentication agent forwarding previously disabled by the 1mrestrict 22moption.

     1mcert-authority0m
             Specifies that the listed key is a certification authority (CA) that is trusted to val‐
             idate signed certificates for user authentication.

             Certificates may encode access restrictions similar to these key options.  If both cer‐
             tificate  restrictions  and  key options are present, the most restrictive union of the
             two is applied.

     1mcommand="command"0m
             Specifies that the command is executed whenever this key is  used  for  authentication.
             The  command  supplied by the user (if any) is ignored.  The command is run on a pty if
             the client requests a pty; otherwise it is run without a tty.  If an 8-bit clean  chan‐
             nel  is  required, one must not request a pty or should specify 1mno-pty22m.  A quote may be
             included in the command by quoting it with a backslash.

             This option might be useful to restrict certain public keys to perform just a  specific
             operation.   An  example  might  be a key that permits remote backups but nothing else.
             Note that the client may specify TCP and/or X11 forwarding unless they  are  explicitly
             prohibited, e.g. using the 1mrestrict 22mkey option.

             The  command originally supplied by the client is available in the 4mSSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND0m
             environment variable.  Note that this option applies to shell, command or subsystem ex‐
             ecution.   Also  note  that  this  command  may  be  superseded  by  an  8;;man:sshd_config(5)4msshd_config24m(5)8;;
             1mForceCommand 22mdirective.

             If  a  command  is specified and a forced-command is embedded in a certificate used for
             authentication, then the certificate will be accepted only  if  the  two  commands  are
             identical.

     1menvironment="NAME=value"0m
             Specifies  that the string is to be added to the environment when logging in using this
             key.  Environment variables set this way override  other  default  environment  values.
             Multiple options of this type are permitted.  Environment processing is disabled by de‐
             fault and is controlled via the 1mPermitUserEnvironment 22moption.

     1mexpiry-time="timespec"0m
             Specifies  a  time after which the key will not be accepted.  The time may be specified
             as a YYYYMMDD[Z] date or a YYYYMMDDHHMM[SS][Z] time.  Dates and times  will  be  inter‐
             preted  in  the  system  time zone unless suffixed by a Z character, in which case they
             will be interpreted in the UTC time zone.

     1mfrom="pattern-list"0m
             Specifies that in addition to public key authentication, either the canonical  name  of
             the  remote  host or its IP address must be present in the comma-separated list of pat‐
             terns.  See PATTERNS in 8;;man:ssh_config(5)4mssh_config24m(5)8;; for more information on patterns.

             In addition to the wildcard matching that may be applied to hostnames or  addresses,  a
             1mfrom 22mstanza may match IP addresses using CIDR address/masklen notation.

             The  purpose  of this option is to optionally increase security: public key authentica‐
             tion by itself does not trust the network or name servers or anything  (but  the  key);
             however, if somebody somehow steals the key, the key permits an intruder to log in from
             anywhere  in the world.  This additional option makes using a stolen key more difficult
             (name servers and/or routers would have to be compromised in addition to just the key).

     1mno-agent-forwarding0m
             Forbids authentication agent forwarding when this key is used for authentication.

     1mno-port-forwarding0m
             Forbids TCP forwarding when this key is used for authentication.  Any port forward  re‐
             quests by the client will return an error.  This might be used, e.g. in connection with
             the 1mcommand 22moption.

     1mno-pty  22mPrevents tty allocation (a request to allocate a pty will fail).

     1mno-user-rc0m
             Disables execution of 4m~/.ssh/rc24m.

     1mno-X11-forwarding0m
             Forbids  X11  forwarding when this key is used for authentication.  Any X11 forward re‐
             quests by the client will return an error.

     1mpermitlisten="[host:]port"0m
             Limit remote port forwarding with the 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;; 1m-R 22moption such that it may only listen  on
             the  specified  host (optional) and port.  IPv6 addresses can be specified by enclosing
             the address in square brackets.  Multiple 1mpermitlisten 22moptions may be applied separated
             by commas.  Hostnames may include wildcards as described in  the  PATTERNS  section  in
             8;;man:ssh_config(5)4mssh_config24m(5)8;;.   A  port specification of 1m* 22mmatches any port.  Note that the setting of
             1mGatewayPorts 22mmay further restrict listen addresses.  Note that 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;; will send a host‐
             name of “localhost” if a listen host was not specified  when  the  forwarding  was  re‐
             quested,  and that this name is treated differently to the explicit localhost addresses
             “127.0.0.1” and “::1”.

     1mpermitopen="host:port"0m
             Limit local port forwarding with the 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;; 1m-L 22moption such that it may only connect  to
             the  specified host and port.  IPv6 addresses can be specified by enclosing the address
             in square brackets.  Multiple 1mpermitopen 22moptions may be applied  separated  by  commas.
             No  pattern  matching or name lookup is performed on the specified hostnames, they must
             be literal host names and/or addresses.  A port specification of 1m* 22mmatches any port.

     1mport-forwarding0m
             Enable port forwarding previously disabled by the 1mrestrict 22moption.

     1mprincipals="principals"0m
             On a 1mcert-authority 22mline, specifies allowed principals for  certificate  authentication
             as a comma-separated list.  At least one name from the list must appear in the certifi‐
             cate's  list  of principals for the certificate to be accepted.  This option is ignored
             for keys that are not marked as trusted certificate signers  using  the  1mcert-authority0m
             option.

     1mpty     22mPermits tty allocation previously disabled by the 1mrestrict 22moption.

     1mno-touch-required0m
             Do not require demonstration of user presence for signatures made using this key.  This
             option only makes sense for the FIDO authenticator algorithms 1mecdsa-sk 22mand 1med25519-sk22m.

     1mverify-required0m
             Require  that  signatures  made using this key attest that they verified the user, e.g.
             via a PIN.  This option only makes sense for the FIDO authenticator algorithms 1mecdsa-sk0m
             and 1med25519-sk22m.

     1mrestrict0m
             Enable all restrictions, i.e. disable port, agent and X11 forwarding, as well  as  dis‐
             abling  PTY allocation and execution of 4m~/.ssh/rc24m.  If any future restriction capabili‐
             ties are added to authorized_keys files, they will be included in this set.

     1mtunnel="n"0m
             Force a 8;;man:tun(4)4mtun24m(4)8;; device on the server.  Without this option, the  next  available  device
             will be used if the client requests a tunnel.

     1muser-rc0m
             Enables execution of 4m~/.ssh/rc24m previously disabled by the 1mrestrict 22moption.

     1mX11-forwarding0m
             Permits X11 forwarding previously disabled by the 1mrestrict 22moption.

     An example authorized_keys file:

        # Comments are allowed at start of line. Blank lines are allowed.
        # Plain key, no restrictions
        ssh-rsa ...
        # Forced command, disable PTY and all forwarding
        restrict,command="dump /home" ssh-rsa ...
        # Restriction of ssh -L forwarding destinations
        permitopen="192.0.2.1:80",permitopen="192.0.2.2:25" ssh-rsa ...
        # Restriction of ssh -R forwarding listeners
        permitlisten="localhost:8080",permitlisten="[::1]:22000" ssh-rsa ...
        # Configuration for tunnel forwarding
        tunnel="0",command="sh /etc/netstart tun0" ssh-rsa ...
        # Override of restriction to allow PTY allocation
        restrict,pty,command="nethack" ssh-rsa ...
        # Allow FIDO key without requiring touch
        no-touch-required sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com ...
        # Require user-verification (e.g. PIN or biometric) for FIDO key
        verify-required sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com ...
        # Trust CA key, allow touch-less FIDO if requested in certificate
        cert-authority,no-touch-required,principals="user_a" ssh-rsa ...

1mSSH_KNOWN_HOSTS FILE FORMAT0m
     The  4m/etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts24m  and  4m~/.ssh/known_hosts24m  files  contain host public keys for all
     known hosts.  The global file should be prepared by the administrator (optional), and the  per-
     user  file  is maintained automatically: whenever the user connects to an unknown host, its key
     is added to the per-user file.

     Each line in these files contains the following fields: marker (optional), hostnames,  keytype,
     base64-encoded key, comment.  The fields are separated by spaces.

     The marker is optional, but if it is present then it must be one of “@cert-authority”, to indi‐
     cate that the line contains a certification authority (CA) key, or “@revoked”, to indicate that
     the key contained on the line is revoked and must not ever be accepted.  Only one marker should
     be used on a key line.

     Hostnames is a comma-separated list of patterns (‘*’ and ‘?’ act as wildcards); each pattern in
     turn  is matched against the host name.  When 1msshd 22mis authenticating a client, such as when us‐
     ing 1mHostbasedAuthentication22m, this will be the canonical client host name.  When 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;;  is  au‐
     thenticating  a  server,  this will be the host name given by the user, the value of the 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;;
     1mHostkeyAlias  22mif  it  was  specified,  or  the  canonical  server  hostname   if   the   8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;;
     1mCanonicalizeHostname 22moption was used.

     A  pattern may also be preceded by ‘!’ to indicate negation: if the host name matches a negated
     pattern, it is not accepted (by that line) even if it matched another pattern on the  line.   A
     hostname or address may optionally be enclosed within ‘[’ and ‘]’ brackets then followed by ‘:’
     and a non-standard port number.

     Alternately,  hostnames  may  be  stored  in a hashed form which hides host names and addresses
     should the file's contents be disclosed.  Hashed hostnames start with a  ‘|’  character.   Only
     one  hashed hostname may appear on a single line and none of the above negation or wildcard op‐
     erators may be applied.

     The keytype and base64-encoded key are taken directly from the host key; they can be  obtained,
     for  example,  from 4m/etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key.pub24m.  The optional comment field continues to the
     end of the line, and is not used.

     Lines starting with ‘#’ and empty lines are ignored as comments.

     When performing host authentication, authentication is accepted if any matching  line  has  the
     proper  key;  either one that matches exactly or, if the server has presented a certificate for
     authentication, the key of the certification authority that signed the certificate.  For a  key
     to  be trusted as a certification authority, it must use the “@cert-authority” marker described
     above.

     The known hosts file also provides a facility to mark keys as revoked, for example when  it  is
     known that the associated private key has been stolen.  Revoked keys are specified by including
     the  “@revoked” marker at the beginning of the key line, and are never accepted for authentica‐
     tion or as certification authorities, but instead will produce a warning from 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;; when  they
     are encountered.

     It  is  permissible  (but not recommended) to have several lines or different host keys for the
     same names.  This will inevitably happen when short forms of host names from different  domains
     are  put in the file.  It is possible that the files contain conflicting information; authenti‐
     cation is accepted if valid information can be found from either file.

     Note that the lines in these files are typically hundreds of characters  long,  and  you  defi‐
     nitely  don't  want  to type in the host keys by hand.  Rather, generate them by a script, 8;;man:ssh-keyscan(1)4mssh-0m
     4mkeyscan24m(1)8;; or by taking, for example, 4m/etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key.pub24m and adding the  host  names
     at  the  front.   8;;man:ssh-keygen(1)4mssh-keygen24m(1)8;; also offers some basic automated editing for 4m~/.ssh/known_hosts0m
     including removing hosts matching a host name and converting all host  names  to  their  hashed
     representations.

     An example ssh_known_hosts file:

        # Comments allowed at start of line
        cvs.example.net,192.0.2.10 ssh-rsa AAAA1234.....=
        # A hashed hostname
        |1|JfKTdBh7rNbXkVAQCRp4OQoPfmI=|USECr3SWf1JUPsms5AqfD5QfxkM= ssh-rsa
        AAAA1234.....=
        # A revoked key
        @revoked * ssh-rsa AAAAB5W...
        # A CA key, accepted for any host in *.mydomain.com or *.mydomain.org
        @cert-authority *.mydomain.org,*.mydomain.com ssh-rsa AAAAB5W...

1mFILES0m
     4m~/.hushlogin0m
             This  file  is  used  to  suppress  printing  the  last  login  time  and 4m/etc/motd24m, if
             1mPrintLastLog 22mand 1mPrintMotd22m, respectively, are enabled.  It does not  suppress  printing
             of the banner specified by 1mBanner22m.

     4m~/.rhosts0m
             This  file is used for host-based authentication (see 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;; for more information).  On
             some machines this file may need to be world-readable if the user's home  directory  is
             on  an  NFS  partition, because 1msshd 22mreads it as root.  Additionally, this file must be
             owned by the user, and must not have write permissions for  anyone  else.   The  recom‐
             mended  permission  for most machines is read/write for the user, and not accessible by
             others.

     4m~/.shosts0m
             This file is used in exactly the same way as 4m.rhosts24m, but allows host-based authentica‐
             tion without permitting login with rlogin/rsh.

     4m~/.ssh/0m
             This directory is the default location for all user-specific configuration and  authen‐
             tication  information.   There is no general requirement to keep the entire contents of
             this directory secret, but the recommended permissions are read/write/execute  for  the
             user, and not accessible by others.

     4m~/.ssh/authorized_keys0m
             Lists  the  public  keys  (ECDSA, Ed25519, RSA) that can be used for logging in as this
             user.  The format of this file is described above.  The content  of  the  file  is  not
             highly  sensitive, but the recommended permissions are read/write for the user, and not
             accessible by others.

             If this file, the 4m~/.ssh24m directory, or the user's home directory are writable by  other
             users,  then  the  file  could  be modified or replaced by unauthorized users.  In this
             case, 1msshd 22mwill not allow it to be used unless the 1mStrictModes 22moption has been  set  to
             “no”.

     4m~/.ssh/environment0m
             This  file  is  read into the environment at login (if it exists).  It can only contain
             empty lines, comment lines (that start with ‘#’), and  assignment  lines  of  the  form
             name=value.   The  file should be writable only by the user; it need not be readable by
             anyone else.  Environment processing is disabled by default and is controlled  via  the
             1mPermitUserEnvironment 22moption.

     4m~/.ssh/known_hosts0m
             Contains  a  list  of host keys for all hosts the user has logged into that are not al‐
             ready in the systemwide list of known host keys.  The format of this file is  described
             above.   This  file should be writable only by root/the owner and can, but need not be,
             world-readable.

     4m~/.ssh/rc0m
             Contains initialization routines to be run before the user's home directory becomes ac‐
             cessible.  This file should be writable only by the user, and need not be  readable  by
             anyone else.

     4m/etc/hosts.equiv0m
             This file is for host-based authentication (see 8;;man:ssh(1)4mssh24m(1)8;;).  It should only be writable by
             root.

     4m/etc/ssh/moduli0m
             Contains  Diffie-Hellman  groups  used  for the "Diffie-Hellman Group Exchange" key ex‐
             change method.  The file format is described in 8;;man:moduli(5)4mmoduli24m(5)8;;.  If  no  usable  groups  are
             found in this file then fixed internal groups will be used.

     4m/etc/motd0m
             See 8;;man:motd(5)4mmotd24m(5)8;;.

     4m/etc/nologin0m
             If  this  file  exists, 1msshd 22mrefuses to let anyone except root log in.  The contents of
             the file are displayed to anyone trying to log in, and  non-root  connections  are  re‐
             fused.  The file should be world-readable.

     4m/etc/ssh/shosts.equiv0m
             This file is used in exactly the same way as 4mhosts.equiv24m, but allows host-based authen‐
             tication without permitting login with rlogin/rsh.

     4m/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ecdsa_key0m
     4m/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key0m
     4m/etc/ssh/ssh_host_mldsa44_ed25519_key0m
     4m/etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key0m
             These  files  contain  the  private parts of the host keys.  These files should only be
             owned by root, readable only by root, and not accessible to  others.   Note  that  1msshd0m
             does not start if these files are group/world-accessible.

     4m/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ecdsa_key.pub0m
     4m/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub0m
     4m/etc/ssh/ssh_host_mldsa44_ed25519_key.pub0m
     4m/etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key.pub0m
             These  files  contain  the public parts of the host keys.  These files should be world-
             readable but writable only by root.  Their contents should match the respective private
             parts.  These files are not really used for anything; they are provided for the  conve‐
             nience  of  the user so their contents can be copied to known hosts files.  These files
             are created using 8;;man:ssh-keygen(1)4mssh-keygen24m(1)8;;.

     4m/etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts0m
             Systemwide list of known host keys.  This file should be prepared by the system  admin‐
             istrator to contain the public host keys of all machines in the organization.  The for‐
             mat  of  this  file  is described above.  This file should be writable only by root/the
             owner and should be world-readable.

     4m/etc/ssh/sshd_config0m
             Contains configuration data for 1msshd22m.  The file format and  configuration  options  are
             described in 8;;man:sshd_config(5)4msshd_config24m(5)8;;.

     4m/etc/ssh/sshrc0m
             Similar to 4m~/.ssh/rc24m, it can be used to specify machine-specific login-time initializa‐
             tions  globally.   This file should be writable only by root, and should be world-read‐
             able.

     4m/usr/share/empty.sshd0m
             8;;man:chroot(2)4mchroot24m(2)8;; directory used by 1msshd 22mduring privilege separation in the  pre-authentication
             phase.   The  directory  should not contain any files and must be owned by root and not
             group or world-writable.

     4m/run/sshd.pid0m
             Contains the process ID of the 1msshd 22mlistening for connections  (if  there  are  several
             daemons  running  concurrently for different ports, this contains the process ID of the
             one started last).  The content of this file is not sensitive; it  can  be  world-read‐
             able.

1mSEE ALSO0m
