4mTASKSET24m(1)                                  User Commands                                 4mTASKSET24m(1)

1mNAME0m
     taskset - set or retrieve a process's CPU affinity

1mSYNOPSIS0m
     1mtaskset 22m[options] 4mmask24m 4mcommand24m [4margument24m...]

     1mtaskset 22m[options] 1m-p 22m[4mmask24m] 4mpid0m

1mDESCRIPTION0m
     The  1mtaskset 22mcommand is used to set or retrieve the CPU affinity of a running process given its
     4mpid24m, or to launch a new 4mcommand24m with a given CPU affinity. CPU affinity is a scheduler property
     that "bonds" a process to a given set of CPUs on the system. The Linux scheduler will honor the
     given CPU affinity and the process will not run on any other CPUs. Note that the  Linux  sched‐
     uler  also  supports natural CPU affinity: the scheduler attempts to keep processes on the same
     CPU as long as practical for performance reasons. Therefore, forcing a specific CPU affinity is
     useful only in certain applications. The affinity of some processes like kernel per-CPU threads
     cannot be set.

     The CPU affinity is represented as a bitmask, with the lowest order bit  corresponding  to  the
     first logical CPU and the highest order bit corresponding to the last logical CPU. Not all CPUs
     may exist on a given system but a mask may specify more CPUs than are present. A retrieved mask
     will reflect only the bits that correspond to CPUs physically on the system. If an invalid mask
     is  given  (i.e.,  one that corresponds to no valid CPUs on the current system) an error is re‐
     turned. The masks may be specified in hexadecimal (with or without a leading "0x"), or as a CPU
     list with the 1m--cpu-list 22moption. For example,

     1m0x000000010m
         is processor #0,

     1m0x000000030m
         is processors #0 and #1,

     1mFFFFFFFF0m
         is processors #0 through #31,

     1m0x320m
         is processors #1, #4, and #5,

     1m--cpu-list 0-2,60m
         is processors #0, #1, #2, and #6.

     1m--cpu-list 0-10:20m
         is processors #0, #2, #4, #6, #8 and #10. The suffix ":N" specifies stride  in  the  range,
         for example 0-10:3 is interpreted as 0,3,6,9 list.

     When  1mtaskset  22mreturns,  it  is guaranteed that the given program has been scheduled to a legal
     CPU.

1mOPTIONS0m
     1m-a22m, 1m--all-tasks0m
         Set or retrieve the CPU affinity of all the tasks (threads) for a given PID.

     1m-c22m, 1m--cpu-list0m
         Interpret 4mmask24m as numerical list of processors instead of a bitmask. Numbers are  separated
         by commas and may include ranges. For example: 1m0,5,8-1122m.

     1m-p22m, 1m--pid0m
         Operate  on  an  existing PID and do not launch a new task. If PID is zero, then operate on
         the 1mtaskset 22mprocess.

     1m-h22m, 1m--help0m
         Display help text and exit.

     1m-V22m, 1m--version0m
         Display version and exit.

1mUSAGE0m
     The default behavior is to run a new command with a given affinity mask:
         1mtaskset 4m22mmask24m 4mcommand24m [4marguments24m]

     You can also retrieve the CPU affinity of an existing task:
         1mtaskset -p 4m22mpid0m

     Or set it:
         1mtaskset -p 4m22mmask24m 4mpid0m

     When a cpu-list is specified for an existing process, the 1m-p 22mand 1m-c 22moptions must be grouped to‐
     gether:
         1mtaskset -pc 4m22mcpu-list24m 4mpid0m

     The 1m--cpu-list 22mform is applicable only for launching new commands:
         1mtaskset --cpu-list 4m22mcpu-list24m 4mcommand0m

1mPERMISSIONS0m
     A user can change the CPU affinity of a process belonging to the same user. A user must possess
     1mCAP_SYS_NICE 22mto change the CPU affinity of a process belonging to another user. A user can  re‐
     trieve the affinity mask of any process.

1mEXIT STATUS0m
     1mtaskset 22mreturns 0 in its affinity-getting mode as long as the provided PID exists.

     1mtaskset  22mreturns  0 in its affinity-setting mode as long as the underlying 1msched_setaffinity22m(2)
     system call does. The success of the command does not guarantee that the specified  thread  has
     actually  migrated  to the indicated CPU(s), but only that the thread will not migrate to a CPU
     outside the new affinity mask. For example, the affinity of the kernel  thread  kswapd  can  be
     set, but the thread may not immediately migrate and is not guaranteed to ever do so:

     $ ps ax -o comm,psr,pid | grep kswapd
     kswapd0           4      82
     $ sudo taskset -p 1 82
     pid 82’s current affinity mask: 1
     pid 82’s new affinity mask: 1
     $ echo $?
     0
     $ ps ax -o comm,psr,pid | grep kswapd
     kswapd0           4      82
     $ taskset -p 82
     pid 82’s current affinity mask: 1

     In  contrast,  when the user specifies an illegal affinity, taskset will print an error and re‐
     turn 1:

     $ ps ax -o comm,psr,pid | grep ksoftirqd/0
     ksoftirqd/0       0      14
     $ sudo taskset -p 1 14
     pid 14’s current affinity mask: 1
     taskset: failed to set pid 14’s affinity: Invalid argument
     $ echo $?
     1

1mEXAMPLES0m
     Print the current CPU affinity as a list.

     $ taskset -pc 0
     pid 1355988’s current affinity list: 0-47

1mAUTHORS0m
     Written by Robert M. Love.

1mCOPYRIGHT0m
     Copyright Â© 2004 Robert M. Love. This is free software; see the source for copying conditions.
     There is NO warranty; not even for MERCHANTABILITY or FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE.

1mSEE ALSO0m
     1mchrt22m(1), 1mnice22m(1), 1mrenice22m(1), 1msched_getaffinity22m(2), 1msched_setaffinity22m(2)

     See 1msched22m(7) for a description of the Linux scheduling scheme.

1mREPORTING BUGS0m
     For bug reports, use the 34missue tracker 0m<https://github.com/util-linux/util-linux/issues>.

1mAVAILABILITY0m
     The 1mtaskset 22mcommand is part of the util-linux package which can be downloaded from 34mLinux Kernel0m
     34mArchive 0m<https://www.kernel.org/pub/linux/utils/util-linux/>.

1mNAME0m

1mSYNOPSIS0m

     1mtc 22m[ 4mOPTIONS24m ] 1mchain [ add | delete | get ] dev 4m22mDEV24m 1m[ parent 4m22mqdisc-id24m 1m|  root  ]  22mfiltertype  [
     filtertype specific parameters ]

     1mtc  22m[ 4mOPTIONS24m ] 1mchain [ add | delete | get ] block 4m22mBLOCK_INDEX24m filtertype [ filtertype specific
     parameters ]


     1mtc 22m[ 4mOPTIONS24m ] [ 4mFORMAT24m ] 1mqdisc { show | list } [ dev 4m22mDEV24m 1m] [ root | ingress | handle 4m22mQHANDLE24m 1m|0m

     1mtc 22m[ 4mOPTIONS24m ] [ 4mFORMAT24m ] 1mclass show dev 4m22mDEV0m

     1mtc 22m[ 4mOPTIONS24m ] 1mfilter show dev 4m22mDEV0m

     1mtc 22m[ 4mOPTIONS24m ] 1mfilter show block 4m22mBLOCK_INDEX0m

     1mtc 22m[ 4mOPTIONS24m ] 1mchain show dev 4m22mDEV0m

     1mtc 22m[ 4mOPTIONS24m ] 1mchain show block 4m22mBLOCK_INDEX0m


     1mtc 22m[ 4mOPTIONS24m ] 1mmonitor [ file 4m22mFILENAME24m 1m]0m


        4mOPTIONS24m := { 1m[ -force ] -b22m[4match24m] 1m[ filename ] 22m| 1m[ -n22m[4metns24m] name 1m] 22m| 1m[ -N22m[4mumeric24m] 1m] 22m| 1m[ -nm 22m|
     1m-nam22m[4mes24m] 1m] 22m| 1m[ 22m{ 1m-cf 22m| 1m-c22m[4monf24m] } 1m[ filename ] ] [ -t22m[imestamp] 1m] 22m| 1m[ -t22m[short] | 1m[ -o22m[neline] 1m]0m
     | 1m[ -echo ] 22m}

        4mFORMAT24m := { 1m-s22m[4mtatistics24m] | 1m-d22m[4metails24m] | 1m-r22m[4maw24m] | 1m-i22m[4mec24m] | 1m-g22m[4mraph24m] | 1m-j22m[4mson24m] | 1m-p22m[4mretty24m]  |
     1m-col22m[4mor24m] }


1mDESCRIPTION0m
     1mTc  22mis  used  to configure Traffic Control in the Linux kernel. Traffic Control consists of the
     following:


     SHAPING
            When traffic is shaped, its rate of transmission is under control. Shaping may  be  more
            than  lowering the available bandwidth - it is also used to smooth out bursts in traffic
            for better network behaviour. Shaping occurs on egress.


     SCHEDULING
            By scheduling the transmission of packets it is possible to  improve  interactivity  for
            traffic  that  needs it while still guaranteeing bandwidth to bulk transfers. Reordering
            is also called prioritizing, and happens only on egress.


     POLICING
            Whereas shaping deals with transmission of traffic, policing pertains to traffic  arriv‐
            ing. Policing thus occurs on ingress.


     DROPPING
            Traffic  exceeding a set bandwidth may also be dropped forthwith, both on ingress and on
            egress.


     Processing of traffic is controlled by three kinds of objects: qdiscs, classes and filters.


1mQDISCS0m
     1mqdisc 22mis short for 'queueing discipline' and it is elementary to understanding traffic control.
     Whenever the kernel needs to send a packet to an interface, it is 1menqueued 22mto the qdisc config‐
     ured for that interface. Immediately afterwards, the kernel tries to get  as  many  packets  as
     possible from the qdisc, for giving them to the network adaptor driver.

     A  simple  QDISC  is  the  'pfifo' one, which does no processing at all and is a pure First In,
     First Out queue. It does however store traffic when the network interface can't handle  it  mo‐
     mentarily.


1mCLASSES0m
     Some qdiscs can contain classes, which contain further qdiscs - traffic may then be enqueued in
     any  of  the  inner  qdiscs,  which are within the 1mclasses.  22mWhen the kernel tries to dequeue a
     packet from such a 1mclassful qdisc 22mit can come from any of the classes. A qdisc may for  example
     prioritize certain kinds of traffic by trying to dequeue from certain classes before others.


1mFILTERS0m
     A  1mfilter  22mis  used  by a classful qdisc to determine in which class a packet will be enqueued.
     Whenever traffic arrives at a class with subclasses, it needs to be classified. Various methods
     may be employed to do so, one of these are the filters. All filters attached to the  class  are
     called, until one of them returns with a verdict. If no verdict was made, other criteria may be
     available. This differs per qdisc.

     It is important to notice that filters reside 1mwithin 22mqdiscs - they are not masters of what hap‐
     pens.

     The available filters are:

     basic  Filter packets based on an ematch expression. See 1mtc-ematch22m(8) for details.

     bpf    Filter packets using (e)BPF, see 1mtc-bpf22m(8) for details.

     cgroup
            Filter  packets  based  on  the control group of their process. See 1mtc-cgroup22m(8) for de‐
            tails.

     flow, flower
            Flow-based classifiers, filtering packets based on their flow (identified by  selectable
            keys). See 1mtc-flow22m(8) and 1mtc-flower22m(8) for details.

     fw     Filter based on fwmark. Directly maps fwmark value to traffic class. See 1mtc-fw22m(8).

     route  Filter packets based on routing table. See 1mtc-route22m(8) for details.

     u32    Generic filtering on arbitrary packet data, assisted by syntax to abstract common opera‐
            tions. See 1mtc-u3222m(8) for details.

     matchall
            Traffic control filter that matches every packet. See 1mtc-matchall22m(8) for details.


1mQEVENTS0m
     Qdiscs  may  invoke  user-configured  actions when certain interesting events take place in the
     qdisc. Each qevent can either be unused, or can have a block attached to it. To this block  are
     then  attached  filters  using  the "tc block BLOCK_IDX" syntax. The block is executed when the
     qevent associated with the attachment point takes place. For example, packet could be  dropped,
     or delayed, etc., depending on the qdisc and the qevent in question.

     For example:

            tc qdisc add dev eth0 root handle 1: red limit 500K avpkt 1K \
               qevent early_drop block 10
            tc filter add block 10 matchall action mirred egress mirror dev eth1


1mCLASSLESS QDISCS0m
     The classless qdiscs are:

     choke  CHOKe  (CHOose and Keep for responsive flows, CHOose and Kill for unresponsive flows) is
            a classless qdisc designed to both identify  and  penalize  flows  that  monopolize  the
            queue. CHOKe is a variation of RED, and the configuration is similar to RED.

     codel  CoDel  (pronounced "coddle") is an adaptive "no-knobs" active queue management algorithm
            (AQM) scheme that was developed to address the shortcomings of RED and its variants.

     [p|b]fifo
            Simplest usable qdisc, pure First In, First Out behaviour.  Limited  in  packets  or  in
            bytes.

     fq     Fair  Queue Scheduler realises TCP pacing and scales to millions of concurrent flows per
            qdisc.

     fq_codel
            Fair Queuing Controlled Delay is queuing discipline that combines Fair Queuing with  the
            CoDel  AQM  scheme.  FQ_Codel  uses a stochastic model to classify incoming packets into
            different flows and is used to provide a fair share of the bandwidth to  all  the  flows
            using  the  queue. Each such flow is managed by the CoDel queuing discipline. Reordering
            within a flow is avoided since Codel internally uses a FIFO queue.

     fq_pie
            FQ-PIE (Flow Queuing with Proportional Integral controller Enhanced) is a queuing disci‐
            pline that combines Flow Queuing with the PIE AQM scheme. FQ-PIE  uses  a  Jenkins  hash
            function to classify incoming packets into different flows and is used to provide a fair
            share  of  the  bandwidth to all the flows using the qdisc. Each such flow is managed by
            the PIE algorithm.

     gred   Generalized Random Early Detection combines multiple RED queues in order to achieve mul‐
            tiple drop priorities. This is required to realize Assured Forwarding (RFC 2597).

     hhf    Heavy-Hitter Filter differentiates between small flows and the opposite,  heavy-hitters.
            The  goal is to catch the heavy-hitters and move them to a separate queue with less pri‐
            ority so that bulk traffic does not affect the latency of critical traffic.

     ingress
            This is a special qdisc as it applies to incoming traffic on an interface, allowing  for
            it to be filtered and policed.

     mqprio
            The Multiqueue Priority Qdisc is a simple queuing discipline that allows mapping traffic
            flows  to  hardware queue ranges using priorities and a configurable priority to traffic
            class mapping. A traffic class in this context is a  set  of  contiguous  qdisc  classes
            which map 1:1 to a set of hardware exposed queues.

     multiq
            Multiqueue  is  a qdisc optimized for devices with multiple Tx queues. It has been added
            for hardware that wishes to avoid head-of-line blocking.  It will cycle though the bands
            and verify that the hardware queue associated with the band is not stopped prior to  de‐
            queuing a packet.

     netem  Network  Emulator  is  an enhancement of the Linux traffic control facilities that allow
            one to add delay, packet loss, duplication and more  other  characteristics  to  packets
            outgoing from a selected network interface.

     pfifo_fast
            Standard  qdisc  for  'Advanced  Router' enabled kernels. Consists of a three-band queue
            which honors Type of Service flags, as well as the priority that may be  assigned  to  a
            packet.

     pie    Proportional Integral controller-Enhanced (PIE) is a control theoretic active queue man‐
            agement  scheme. It is based on the proportional integral controller but aims to control
            delay.

     red    Random Early Detection simulates physical congestion by randomly dropping  packets  when
            nearing  configured  bandwidth  allocation. Well suited to very large bandwidth applica‐
            tions.

     sfb    Stochastic Fair Blue is a classless qdisc to manage congestion based on packet loss  and
            link  utilization  history while trying to prevent non-responsive flows (i.e. flows that
            do not react to congestion marking or dropped packets) from impacting performance of re‐
            sponsive flows.  Unlike RED, where the marking probability has to  be  configured,  BLUE
            tries to determine the ideal marking probability automatically.

     sfq    Stochastic  Fairness  Queueing  reorders queued traffic so each 'session' gets to send a
            packet in turn.

     tbf    The Token Bucket Filter is suited for slowing traffic down  to  a  precisely  configured
            rate. Scales well to large bandwidths.

1mCONFIGURING CLASSLESS QDISCS0m
     In  the  absence of classful qdiscs, classless qdiscs can only be attached at the root of a de‐
     vice. Full syntax:

     1mtc qdisc add dev 4m22mDEV24m 1mroot 22mQDISC QDISC-PARAMETERS

     To remove, issue

     1mtc qdisc del dev 4m22mDEV24m 1mroot0m

     The 1mpfifo_fast 22mqdisc is the automatic default in the absence of a configured qdisc.


1mCLASSFUL QDISCS0m
     The classful qdiscs are:

     ATM    Map flows to virtual circuits of an underlying asynchronous transfer mode device.

     DRR    The Deficit Round Robin Scheduler is a more flexible replacement for Stochastic Fairness
            Queuing. Unlike SFQ, there are no built-in queues -- you need to add  classes  and  then
            set  up  filters to classify packets accordingly.  This can be useful e.g. for using RED
            qdiscs with different settings for particular traffic. There is no default class -- if a
            packet cannot be classified, it is dropped.

     ETS    The ETS qdisc is a queuing discipline that merges functionality of PRIO and  DRR  qdiscs
            in  one  scheduler. ETS makes it easy to configure a set of strict and bandwidth-sharing
            bands to implement the transmission selection described in 802.1Qaz.

     HFSC   Hierarchical Fair Service Curve guarantees precise bandwidth and  delay  allocation  for
            leaf  classes  and allocates excess bandwidth fairly. Unlike HTB, it makes use of packet
            dropping to achieve low delays which interactive sessions benefit from.

     HTB    The Hierarchy Token Bucket implements a rich linksharing hierarchy of  classes  with  an
            emphasis  on conforming to existing practices. HTB facilitates guaranteeing bandwidth to
            classes, while also allowing specification of upper limits to  inter-class  sharing.  It
            contains shaping elements, based on TBF and can prioritize classes.

     PRIO   The PRIO qdisc is a non-shaping container for a configurable number of classes which are
            dequeued  in  order. This allows for easy prioritization of traffic, where lower classes
            are only able to send if higher ones have no packets available. To facilitate configura‐
            tion, Type Of Service bits are honored by default.

     QFQ    Quick Fair Queueing is an O(1) scheduler that provides near-optimal guarantees,  and  is
            the  first  to achieve that goal with a constant cost also with respect to the number of
            groups and the packet length. The QFQ algorithm has no loops, and uses very  simple  in‐
            structions  and data structures that lend themselves very well to a hardware implementa‐
            tion.

1mTHEORY OF OPERATION0m
     Classes form a tree, where each class has a single parent.  A class may have multiple children.
     Some qdiscs allow for runtime addition of classes (HTB) while others (PRIO) are created with  a
     static number of children.

     Qdiscs  which allow dynamic addition of classes can have zero or more subclasses to which traf‐
     fic may be enqueued.

     Furthermore, each class contains a 1mleaf qdisc 22mwhich by default has  1mpfifo  22mbehaviour,  although
     another  qdisc  can  be attached in place. This qdisc may again contain classes, but each class
     can have only one leaf qdisc.

     When a packet enters a classful qdisc it can be 1mclassified 22mto one of the classes within.  Three
     criteria are available, although not all qdiscs will use all three:

     tc filters
            If  tc  filters  are attached to a class, they are consulted first for relevant instruc‐
            tions. Filters can match on all fields of a packet header, as well as  on  the  firewall
            mark applied by iptables.

     Type of Service
            Some qdiscs have built in rules for classifying packets based on the TOS field.

     skb->priority
            Userspace  programs can encode a 4mclass-id24m in the 'skb->priority' field using the SO_PRI‐
            ORITY option.

     Each node within the tree can have its own filters but higher level filters may also point  di‐
     rectly to lower classes.

     If  classification  did  not  succeed,  packets are enqueued to the leaf qdisc attached to that
     class. Check qdisc specific manpages for details, however.


1mNAMING0m
     All qdiscs, classes and filters have IDs, which can either be specified or be automatically as‐
     signed.

     IDs consist of a 1mmajor 22mnumber and a 1mminor 22mnumber, separated by a colon - 1mmajor22m:1mminor22m.  Both 1mma‐0m
     1mjor 22mand 1mminor 22mare hexadecimal numbers and are limited to 16 bits. There are two special values:
     root is signified by 1mmajor 22mand 1mminor 22mof all ones, and unspecified is all zeros.


     QDISCS
            A qdisc, which potentially can have children, gets assigned a  1mmajor  22mnumber,  called  a
            'handle',  leaving  the  1mminor 22mnumber namespace available for classes. The handle is ex‐
            pressed as '10:'.  It is customary to explicitly assign a handle to qdiscs  expected  to
            have children.


     CLASSES
            Classes  residing under a qdisc share their qdisc 1mmajor 22mnumber, but each have a separate
            1mminor 22mnumber called a 'classid' that has no relation to their parent  classes,  only  to
            their parent qdisc. The same naming custom as for qdiscs applies.


     FILTERS
            Filters have a three part ID, which is only needed when using a hashed filter hierarchy.


1mPARAMETERS0m
     The following parameters are widely used in TC. For other parameters, see the man pages for in‐
     dividual qdiscs.


     RATES  Bandwidths or rates.  These parameters accept a floating point number, possibly followed
            by either a unit (both SI and IEC units supported), or a float followed by a '%' charac‐
            ter to specify the rate as a percentage of the device's speed (e.g. 5%, 99.5%). Warning:
            specifying  the rate as a percentage means a fraction of the current speed; if the speed
            changes, the value will not be recalculated.

            bit or a bare number
                   Bits per second

            kbit   Kilobits per second

            mbit   Megabits per second

            gbit   Gigabits per second

            tbit   Terabits per second

            bps    Bytes per second

            kbps   Kilobytes per second

            mbps   Megabytes per second

            gbps   Gigabytes per second

            tbps   Terabytes per second


            To specify in IEC units, replace the SI prefix (k-, m-, g-, t-) with  IEC  prefix  (ki-,
            mi-, gi- and ti-) respectively.


            TC  store  rates as a 32-bit unsigned integer in bps internally, so we can specify a max
            rate of 4294967295 bps.


     TIMES  Length of time. Can be specified as a floating point  number  followed  by  an  optional
            unit:

            s, sec or secs
                   Whole seconds

            ms, msec or msecs
                   Milliseconds

            us, usec, usecs or a bare number
                   Microseconds.


            TC defined its own time unit (equal to microsecond) and stores time values as 32-bit un‐
            signed integer, thus we can specify a max time value of 4294967295 usecs.


     SIZES  Amounts  of  data.  Can  be specified as a floating point number followed by an optional
            unit:

            b or a bare number
                   Bytes.

            kbit   Kilobits

            kb or k
                   Kilobytes

            mbit   Megabits

            mb or m
                   Megabytes

            gbit   Gigabits

            gb or g
                   Gigabytes


            TC stores sizes internally as 32-bit unsigned integer in byte, so we can specify  a  max
            size of 4294967295 bytes.


     VALUES
            Other  values  without  a unit.  These parameters are interpreted as decimal by default,
            but you can indicate TC to interpret them as octal and hexadecimal by adding  a  '0'  or
            '0x' prefix respectively.


1mTC COMMANDS0m
     The following commands are available for qdiscs, classes and filter:

     add    Add  a  qdisc, class or filter to a node. For all entities, a 1mparent 22mmust be passed, ei‐
            ther by passing its ID or by attaching directly to the root of a device.  When  creating
            a  qdisc  or  a filter, it can be named with the 1mhandle 22mparameter. A class is named with
            the 1mclassid 22mparameter.


     delete
            A qdisc can be deleted by specifying its handle, which may  also  be  'root'.  All  sub‐
            classes and their leaf qdiscs are automatically deleted, as well as any filters attached
            to them.


     change
            Some entities can be modified 'in place'. Shares the syntax of 'add', with the exception
            that  the  handle  cannot  be changed and neither can the parent. In other words, 1mchange0m
            cannot move a node.


     replace
            Performs a nearly atomic remove/add on an existing node id. If the node does  not  exist
            yet it is created.


     get    Displays  a single filter given the interface 4mDEV24m, 4mqdisc-id24m, 4mpriority24m, 4mprotocol24m and 4mfil‐0m
            4mter-id24m.


     show   Displays all filters attached to the given interface. A valid parent ID must be passed.


     link   Only available for qdiscs and performs a replace where the node must exist already.


1mMONITOR0m
     The 1mtc 22mutility can monitor events generated by the kernel such as adding/deleting qdiscs,  fil‐
     ters or actions, or modifying existing ones.

     The following command is available for 1mmonitor 22m:

     1mfile   22mIf  the  file  option  is  given, the 1mtc 22mdoes not listen to kernel events, but opens the
            given file and dumps its contents. The file has to  be  in  binary  format  and  contain
            netlink messages.


1mOPTIONS0m
     1m-b22m, 1m-b filename22m, 1m-batch22m, 1m-batch filename0m
            read  commands from provided file or standard input and invoke them.  First failure will
            cause termination of tc.


     1m-force0m
            don't terminate tc on errors in batch mode.  If there were any errors  during  execution
            of the commands, the application return code will be non zero.


     1m-o22m, 1m-oneline0m
            output  each  record on a single line, replacing line feeds with the 1m'\' 22mcharacter. This
            is convenient when you want to count records with 1mwc22m(1) or to 1mgrep22m(1) the output.


     1m-n22m, 1m-net22m, 1m-netns 22m<NETNS>
            switches 1mtc 22mto the specified network namespace 4mNETNS24m.  Actually it just simplifies  exe‐
            cuting of:

            1mip netns exec 4m22mNETNS24m 1mtc 22m[ 4mOPTIONS24m ] 4mOBJECT24m { 4mCOMMAND24m | 1mhelp 22m}

            to

            1mtc 22m-n[etns] 4mNETNS24m [ 4mOPTIONS24m ] 4mOBJECT24m { 4mCOMMAND24m | 1mhelp 22m}


     1m-N22m, 1m-Numeric0m
            Print  the  number of protocol, scope, dsfield, etc directly instead of converting it to
            human readable name.


     1m-cf22m, 1m-conf 22m<FILENAME>
            specifies path to the config file. This option is used in conjunction with other options
            (e.g.  1m-nm22m).


     1m-t22m, 1m-timestamp0m
            When 1mtc monitor 22mruns, print timestamp before the event message in format:
               Timestamp: <Day> <Month> <DD> <hh:mm:ss> <YYYY> <usecs> usec


     1m-ts22m, 1m-tshort0m
            When 1mtc monitor 22mruns, prints short timestamp before the event message in format:
               [<YYYY>-<MM>-<DD>T<hh:mm:ss>.<ms>]


     1m-echo  22mRequest the kernel to send the applied configuration back.


1mFORMAT0m
     The show command has additional formatting options:


     1m-s22m, 1m-stats22m, 1m-statistics0m
            output more statistics about packet usage.


     1m-d22m, 1m-details0m
            output more detailed information about rates and cell sizes.


     1m-r22m, 1m-raw0m
            output raw hex values for handles.


     1m-p22m, 1m-pretty0m
            for u32 filter, decode offset and mask values to equivalent  filter  commands  based  on
            TCP/IP.  In JSON output, add whitespace to improve readability.


     1m-iec   22mprint rates in IEC units (ie. 1K = 1024).


     1m-g22m, 1m-graph0m
            shows  classes  as  ASCII graph. Prints generic stats info under each class if 1m-s 22moption
            was specified. Classes can be filtered only by 1mdev 22moption.


     1m-c22m[1mcolor22m][1m=22m{1malways22m|1mauto22m|1mnever22m}
            Configure color output. If parameter is omitted or 1malways22m, color output is  enabled  re‐
            gardless  of  stdout state. If parameter is 1mauto22m, stdout is checked to be a terminal be‐
            fore enabling color output. If parameter is 1mnever22m, color output is disabled.  If  speci‐
            fied  multiple  times,  the  last one takes precedence. This flag is ignored if 1m-json 22mis
            also given.


     1m-j22m, 1m-json0m
            Display results in JSON format.


     1m-nm22m, 1m-name0m
            resolve class name from 1m/etc/iproute2/tc_cls 22mfile or from file specified by 1m-cf  22moption.
            This file is just a mapping of 1mclassid 22mto class name:

               # Here is comment
               1:40   voip # Here is another comment
               1:50   web
               1:60   ftp
               1:2    home

            1mtc  22mwill  not fail if 1m-nm 22mwas specified without 1m-cf 22moption but 1m/etc/iproute2/tc_cls 22mfile
            does not exist, which makes it possible to pass 1m-nm 22moption for creating 1mtc 22malias.


     1m-br22m, 1m-brief0m
            Print only essential data needed to identify the  filter  and  action  (handle,  cookie,
            etc.)  and  stats.  This option is currently only supported by 1mtc filter show 22mand 1mtc ac‐0m
            1mtions ls 22mcommands.


1mEXAMPLES0m
     tc -g class show dev eth0
         Shows classes as ASCII graph on eth0 interface.

     tc -g -s class show dev eth0
         Shows classes as ASCII graph with stats info under each class.


1mHISTORY0m
     1mtc 22mwas written by Alexey N. Kuznetsov and added in Linux 2.2.

1mSEE ALSO0m
     1mtc-basic22m(8), 1mtc-bfifo22m(8), 1mtc-bpf22m(8), 1mtc-cake22m(8), 1mtc-cgroup22m(8),  1mtc-choke22m(8),  1mtc-codel22m(8),  1mtc-0m
     1mdrr22m(8),  1mtc-ematch22m(8),  1mtc-ets22m(8),  1mtc-flow22m(8),  1mtc-flower22m(8),  1mtc-fq22m(8),  1mtc-fq_codel22m(8),  1mtc-0m
     1mfq_pie22m(8), 1mtc-fw22m(8), 1mtc-gact22m(8), 1mtc-hfsc22m(7), 1mtc-hfsc22m(8), 1mtc-htb22m(8), 1mtc-mqprio22m(8),  1mtc-pfifo22m(8),
     1mtc-pfifo_fast22m(8),  1mtc-pie22m(8),  1mtc-red22m(8),  1mtc-route22m(8),  1mtc-sfb22m(8),  1mtc-sfq22m(8), 1mtc-stab22m(8), 1mtc-0m
     1mtbf22m(8), 1mtc-u3222m(8)
     User documentation at 1mhttp://lartc.org/22m, but please direct bugreports  and  patches  to:  1m<net‐0m
     1mdev@vger.kernel.org>0m

4mTEST24m(1)                                     User Commands                                    4mTEST24m(1)

1mNAME0m
     test - check file types and compare values

1mSYNOPSIS0m
     1mtest 4m22mEXPRESSION0m
     1mtest0m
     1m[ 4m22mEXPRESSION24m 1m]0m
     1m[ ]0m
     1m[ 4m22mOPTION0m

1mDESCRIPTION0m
     Exit with the status determined by EXPRESSION.

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/test#test--help1m--help22m8;;
            display this help and exit

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/test#test--version1m--version22m8;;
            output version information and exit

     An  omitted EXPRESSION defaults to false.  Otherwise, EXPRESSION is true or false and sets exit
     status.  It is one of:

     ( EXPRESSION )               EXPRESSION is true
     ! EXPRESSION                 EXPRESSION is false
     EXPRESSION1 1m-a 22mEXPRESSION2   both EXPRESSION1 and EXPRESSION2 are true
     EXPRESSION1 1m-o 22mEXPRESSION2   either EXPRESSION1 or EXPRESSION2 is true

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-n1m-n STRING22m8;;                    the length of STRING is nonzero

     STRING                       equivalent to 1m-n 22mSTRING

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-z1m-z STRING22m8;;                    the length of STRING is zero
     STRING1 = STRING2    the strings are equal
     STRING1 != STRING2   the strings are not equal
     STRING1 > STRING2    STRING1 is greater than STRING2 in the current locale
     STRING1 < STRING2    STRING1 is less than STRING2 in the current locale

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-eq1mINTEGER1 -eq INTEGER222m8;;   INTEGER1 is equal to INTEGER2
     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-ge1mINTEGER1 -ge INTEGER222m8;;   INTEGER1 is greater than or equal to INTEGER2
     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-gt1mINTEGER1 -gt INTEGER222m8;;   INTEGER1 is greater than INTEGER2
     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-le1mINTEGER1 -le INTEGER222m8;;   INTEGER1 is less than or equal to INTEGER2
     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-lt1mINTEGER1 -lt INTEGER222m8;;   INTEGER1 is less than INTEGER2
     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-ne1mINTEGER1 -ne INTEGER222m8;;   INTEGER1 is not equal to INTEGER2

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-ef1mFILE1 -ef FILE222m8;;   FILE1 and FILE2 have the same device and inode numbers
     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-nt1mFILE1 -nt FILE222m8;;   FILE1 is newer (modification date) than FILE2
     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-ot1mFILE1 -ot FILE222m8;;   FILE1 is older than FILE2

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-b1m-b FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and is block special

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-c1m-c FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and is character special

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-d1m-d FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and is a directory

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-e1m-e FILE22m8;;           FILE exists

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-f1m-f FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and is a regular file

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-g1m-g FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and its set-group-ID bit is set

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-G1m-G FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and is owned by the effective group ID

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-h1m-h FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and is a symbolic link (same as 1m-L22m)

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-k1m-k FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and has its sticky bit set

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-L1m-L FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and is a symbolic link (same as 1m-h22m)

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-N1m-N FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and has been modified since it was last read

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-O1m-O FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and is owned by the effective user ID

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-p1m-p FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and is a named pipe

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-r1m-r FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and the user has read access

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-s1m-s FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and has a size greater than zero

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-S1m-S FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and is a socket

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-t1m-t FD22m8;;             file descriptor FD is opened on a terminal

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-u1m-u FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and its set-user-ID bit is set

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-w1m-w FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and the user has write access

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#test-x1m-x FILE22m8;;           FILE exists and the user has execute (or search) access

     Except for 1m-h 22mand 1m-L22m, all FILE-related tests dereference symbolic links.  Beware that parenthe‐
     ses need to be escaped (e.g., by backslashes) for shells.  INTEGER may also be 1m-l 22mSTRING, which
     evaluates to the length of STRING.

     Binary 1m-a 22mand 1m-o 22mare ambiguous.  Use 'test EXPR1 && test EXPR2' or 'test EXPR1 ||  test  EXPR2'
     instead.

     '[' honors 1m--help 22mand 1m--version22m, but 'test' treats them as STRINGs.

     Your  shell may have its own version of test and/or [, which usually supersedes the version de‐
     scribed here.  Please refer to your shell's documentation for details about the options it sup‐
     ports.

4mTIMEDATECTL24m(1)                               timedatectl                              4mTIMEDATECTL24m(1)

1mNAME0m
     timedatectl - Control the system time and date

1mSYNOPSIS0m
     1mtimedatectl 22m[OPTIONS...] {COMMAND}

1mDESCRIPTION0m
     1mtimedatectl  22mmay  be  used to query and change the system clock and its settings, and enable or
     disable time synchronization services.

     Use 1msystemd-firstboot22m(1) to initialize the system time zone for mounted (but not booted) system
     images.

     1mtimedatectl 22mmay be used to show the current status of time synchronization services, for  exam‐
     ple 1msystemd-timesyncd.service22m(8).

1mCOMMANDS0m
     The following commands are understood:

     1mstatus0m
         Show  current settings of the system clock and RTC, including whether network time synchro‐
         nization is active. If no command is specified, this is the implied default.

         Added in version 195.

     1mshow0m
         Show the same information as 1mstatus22m, but in machine readable form. This command is intended
         to be used whenever computer-parsable output is required. Use 1mstatus 22mif you are looking for
         formatted human-readable output.

         By default, empty properties are suppressed. Use 1m--all 22mto show those too.  To  select  spe‐
         cific properties to show, use 1m--property=22m.

         Added in version 239.

     1mset-time [TIME]0m
         Set the system clock to the specified timestamp. This will also update the RTC time accord‐
         ingly.  The  timestamp  may  be  specified  in  the  format "2012-10-30 18:17:16". See 1msys‐0m
         1mtemd.time22m(7) for more details about acceptable timestamp format.

         Added in version 195.

     1mset-timezone [TIMEZONE]0m
         Set the system time zone to the specified value. Available timezones  can  be  listed  with
         1mlist-timezones22m. If the RTC is configured to be in the local time, this will also update the
         RTC time. This call will alter the /etc/localtime symlink. See 1mlocaltime22m(5) for more infor‐
         mation.

         Added in version 195.

     1mlist-timezones0m
         List  available  time  zones,  one per line. Entries from the list can be set as the system
         timezone with 1mset-timezone22m.

         Added in version 195.

     1mset-local-rtc [BOOL]0m
         Takes a boolean argument. If "0", the system is configured to maintain the RTC in universal
         time. If "1", it will maintain the RTC in local time instead. Note that maintaining the RTC
         in the local timezone is not fully supported and will create  various  problems  with  time
         zone changes and daylight saving adjustments. If at all possible, keep the RTC in UTC mode.
         Note  that  invoking this will also synchronize the RTC from the system clock, unless 1m--ad‐0m
         1mjust-system-clock 22mis passed (see above). This command will change the 3rd line of /etc/adj‐
         time, as documented in 1mhwclock22m(8).

         Added in version 195.

     1mset-ntp [BOOL]0m
         Takes a boolean argument. Controls whether network time synchronization is active  and  en‐
         abled  (if  available). If the argument is true, this enables and starts the first existing
         network synchronization service. If the argument is false, then this disables and stops the
         known network synchronization services. The way that the list of services is built  is  de‐
         scribed in 1msystemd-timedated.service22m(8).

         Added in version 195.

   1msystemd-timesyncd Commands0m
     The following commands are specific to 1msystemd-timesyncd.service22m(8).

     1mtimesync-status0m
         Show  current  status of 1msystemd-timesyncd.service22m(8). If 1m--monitor 22mis specified, then this
         will monitor the status updates.

         Added in version 239.

     1mshow-timesync0m
         Show the same information as 1mtimesync-status22m, but in machine readable form. This command is
         intended to be used whenever computer-parsable output is required. Use  1mtimesync-status  22mif
         you are looking for formatted human-readable output.

         By  default,  empty  properties are suppressed. Use 1m--all 22mto show those too. To select spe‐
         cific properties to show, use 1m--property=22m.

         Added in version 239.

     1mntp-servers 4m22mINTERFACE24m 4mSERVER24m1m...0m
         Set the interface specific NTP servers. This command can be used only when the interface is
         managed by 1msystemd-networkd22m.

         Added in version 243.

     1mrevert 4m22mINTERFACE0m
         Revert the interface specific NTP servers. This command can be used only when the interface
         is managed by 1msystemd-networkd22m.

         Added in version 243.

1mOPTIONS0m
     The following options are understood:

     1m--adjust-system-clock0m
         If 1mset-local-rtc 22mis invoked and this option is passed, the  system  clock  is  synchronized
         from the RTC again, taking the new setting into account. Otherwise, the RTC is synchronized
         from the system clock.

         Added in version 195.

     1m--monitor0m
         If 1mtimesync-status 22mis invoked and this option is passed, then 1mtimedatectl 22mmonitors the sta‐
         tus  of  1msystemd-timesyncd.service22m(8)  and updates the outputs. Use Ctrl+C to terminate the
         monitoring.

         Added in version 239.

     1m-a22m, 1m--all0m
         When showing properties of 1msystemd-timesyncd.service22m(8), show all properties regardless  of
         whether they are set or not.

         Added in version 239.

     1m-p22m, 1m--property=0m
         When  showing  properties of 1msystemd-timesyncd.service22m(8), limit display to certain proper‐
         ties as specified as argument. If not specified, all set properties are shown. The argument
         should be a property name, such as "ServerName". If specified more than once,  all  proper‐
         ties with the specified names are shown.

         Added in version 239.

     1m--value0m
         When  printing  properties  with 1mshow-timesync22m, only print the value, and skip the property
         name and "=".

         Added in version 239.

     1m-P0m
         Equivalent to 1m--value --property=22m, i.e. shows the value of the property without  the  prop‐
         erty  name  or  "=".  Note  that  using 1m-P 22monce will also affect all properties listed with
         1m-p22m/1m--property=22m.

         Added in version 256.

     1m-H22m, 1m--host=0m
         Execute the operation remotely. Specify a hostname, or a username and hostname separated by
         "@", to connect to. The hostname may optionally be suffixed by a port ssh is listening  on,
         separated by ":", and then a container name, separated by "/", which connects directly to a
         specific  container  on the specified host. This will use SSH to talk to the remote machine
         manager instance. Container names may be enumerated with 1mmachinectl -H 4m22mHOST24m. Put  IPv6  ad‐
         dresses in brackets.

     1m-M22m, 1m--machine=0m
         Execute  operation on a local container. Specify a container name to connect to, optionally
         prefixed by a user name to connect as and a separating "@" character. If the special string
         ".host" is used in place of the container name, a connection to the local  system  is  made
         (which   is   useful   to   connect   to   a   specific  user's  user  bus:  "--user  --ma‐
         chine=lennart@.host"). If the "@" syntax is not used, the connection is made as root  user.
         If  the  "@" syntax is used either the left hand side or the right hand side may be omitted
         (but not both) in which case the local user name and ".host" are implied.

     1m--no-ask-password0m
         Do not query the user for authentication for privileged operations.

     1m-h22m, 1m--help0m
         Print a short help text and exit.

     1m--version0m
         Print a short version string and exit.

     1m--no-pager0m
         Do not pipe output into a pager.

1mEXIT STATUS0m
     On success, 0 is returned, a non-zero failure code otherwise.

1mENVIRONMENT0m
     4m$SYSTEMD_LOG_LEVEL0m
         The maximum log level of emitted messages (messages with a higher log level, i.e. less  im‐
         portant  ones,  will be suppressed). Takes a comma-separated list of values. A value may be
         either one of (in order of decreasing importance) 1memerg22m, 1malert22m, 1mcrit22m, 1merr22m, 1mwarning22m, 1mnotice22m,
         1minfo22m, 1mdebug22m, or an integer in the range 0...7. See 1msyslog22m(3)  for  more  information.  Each
         value may optionally be prefixed with one of 1mconsole22m, 1msyslog22m, 1mkmsg 22mor 1mjournal 22mfollowed by a
         colon   to   set   the  maximum  log  level  for  that  specific  log  target  (e.g.   1mSYS‐0m
         1mTEMD_LOG_LEVEL=debug,console:info 22mspecifies to log at debug level except  when  logging  to
         the  console  which  should be at info level). Note that the global maximum log level takes
         priority over any per target maximum log levels.

     4m$SYSTEMD_LOG_COLOR0m
         A boolean. If true, messages written to the tty will be colored according to priority.

         This setting is only useful when messages are written directly  to  the  terminal,  because
         1mjournalctl22m(1)  and other tools that display logs will color messages based on the log level
         on their own.

     4m$SYSTEMD_LOG_TIME0m
         A boolean. If true, console log messages will be prefixed with a timestamp.

         This setting is only useful when messages are written directly to the terminal or  a  file,
         because 1mjournalctl22m(1) and other tools that display logs will attach timestamps based on the
         entry metadata on their own.

     4m$SYSTEMD_LOG_LOCATION0m
         A boolean. If true, messages will be prefixed with a filename and line number in the source
         code where the message originates.

         Note that the log location is often attached as metadata to journal entries anyway. Includ‐
         ing it directly in the message text can nevertheless be convenient when debugging programs.

     4m$SYSTEMD_LOG_TID0m
         A boolean. If true, messages will be prefixed with the current numerical thread ID (TID).

         Note that the this information is attached as metadata to journal entries anyway. Including
         it directly in the message text can nevertheless be convenient when debugging programs.

     4m$SYSTEMD_LOG_TARGET0m
         The  destination  for  log messages. One of 1mconsole 22m(log to the attached tty), 1mconsole-pre‐0m
         1mfixed 22m(log to the attached tty but with prefixes encoding the log level and "facility", see
         1msyslog22m(3), 1mkmsg 22m(log to the kernel circular log buffer),  1mjournal  22m(log  to  the  journal),
         1mjournal-or-kmsg  22m(log  to the journal if available, and to kmsg otherwise), 1mauto 22m(determine
         the appropriate log target automatically, the default), 1mnull 22m(disable log output).

     4m$SYSTEMD_LOG_RATELIMIT_KMSG0m
         Whether to ratelimit kmsg or not. Takes a boolean. Defaults to "true". If disabled, systemd
         will not ratelimit messages written to kmsg.

     4m$SYSTEMD_PAGER24m, 4m$PAGER0m
         Pager to use when 1m--no-pager 22mis not given.  4m$SYSTEMD_PAGER24m is used if set; otherwise 4m$PAGER0m
         is used. If neither 4m$SYSTEMD_PAGER24m nor 4m$PAGER24m are set, a set of well-known pager  implemen‐
         tations  is  tried  in turn, including 1mless22m(1) and 1mmore22m(1), until one is found. If no pager
         implementation is discovered, no pager is invoked. Setting those environment  variables  to
         an empty string or the value "cat" is equivalent to passing 1m--no-pager22m.

         Note:  if  4m$SYSTEMD_PAGERSECURE24m  is  not set, 4m$SYSTEMD_PAGER24m and 4m$PAGER24m can only be used to
         disable the pager (with "cat" or ""), and are otherwise ignored.

     4m$SYSTEMD_LESS0m
         Override the options passed to 1mless 22m(by default "FRSXMK").

         Users might want to change two options in particular:

         1mK0m
             This option instructs the pager to exit immediately when Ctrl+C is  pressed.  To  allow
             1mless 22mto handle Ctrl+C itself to switch back to the pager command prompt, unset this op‐
             tion.

             If  the  value  of 4m$SYSTEMD_LESS24m does not include "K", and the pager that is invoked is
             1mless22m, Ctrl+C will be ignored by the executable, and needs to be handled by the pager.

         1mX0m
             This option instructs the pager to not send termcap initialization and deinitialization
             strings to the terminal. It is set by default to allow command output to remain visible
             in the terminal even after the pager exits.  Nevertheless,  this  prevents  some  pager
             functionality  from  working,  in  particular  paged output cannot be scrolled with the
             mouse.

         Note that setting the regular 4m$LESS24m environment variable has no effect for 1mless 22minvocations
         by systemd tools.

         See 1mless22m(1) for more discussion.

     4m$SYSTEMD_LESSCHARSET0m
         Override the charset passed to 1mless 22m(by default "utf-8", if the invoking terminal is deter‐
         mined to be UTF-8 compatible).

         Note that setting the regular 4m$LESSCHARSET24m environment variable has no effect for 1mless  22min‐
         vocations by systemd tools.

     4m$SYSTEMD_PAGERSECURE0m
         Common  pager  commands  like  1mless22m(1), in addition to "paging", i.e. scrolling through the
         output, support opening of or writing to other files and running arbitrary shell  commands.
         When commands are invoked with elevated privileges, for example under 1msudo22m(8) or 1mpkexec22m(1),
         the  pager becomes a security boundary. Care must be taken that only programs with strictly
         limited functionality are used as pagers, and unintended interactive features like  opening
         or creation of new files or starting of subprocesses are not allowed. "Secure mode" for the
         pager  may  be  enabled as described below, 4mif24m 4mthe24m 4mpager24m 4msupports24m 4mthat24m (most pagers are not
         written in a way that takes this into consideration). It is recommended to  either  explic‐
         itly  enable "secure mode" or to completely disable the pager using 1m--no-pager 22mor 4mPAGER=cat0m
         when allowing untrusted users to execute commands with elevated privileges.

         This option takes a boolean argument. When set to true, the "secure mode" of the  pager  is
         enabled.  In  "secure  mode",  1mLESSSECURE=1  22mwill be set when invoking the pager, which in‐
         structs the pager to disable commands that open or create  new  files  or  start  new  sub‐
         processes.  Currently  only 1mless22m(1) is known to understand this variable and implement "se‐
         cure mode".

         When set to false, no limitation is placed on the pager. Setting  4mSYSTEMD_PAGERSECURE=024m  or
         not  removing it from the inherited environment may allow the user to invoke arbitrary com‐
         mands.

         When 4m$SYSTEMD_PAGERSECURE24m is not set, systemd tools attempt to automatically figure out  if
         "secure mode" should be enabled and whether the pager supports it. "Secure mode" is enabled
         if  the effective UID is not the same as the owner of the login session, see 1mgeteuid22m(2) and
         1msd_pid_get_owner_uid22m(3), or when running under 1msudo22m(8) or similar tools (4m$SUDO_UID24m  is  set
         [1]).  In  those cases, 4mSYSTEMD_PAGERSECURE=124m will be set and pagers which are not known to
         implement "secure mode" will not be used at all. Note that this autodetection  only  covers
         the most common mechanisms to elevate privileges and is intended as convenience. It is rec‐
         ommended to explicitly set 4m$SYSTEMD_PAGERSECURE24m or disable the pager.

         Note  that if the 4m$SYSTEMD_PAGER24m or 4m$PAGER24m variables are to be honoured, other than to dis‐
         able the pager, 4m$SYSTEMD_PAGERSECURE24m must be set too.

     4m$SYSTEMD_COLORS0m
         Takes a boolean argument, or a special value. By default (unset), 1msystemd 22mand related util‐
         ities will use colors in their output if possible. If 4m$COLORTERM24m is set to  "truecolor"  or
         "24bit", 24-bit colors will be enabled, 256 colors otherwise, unless 4m$NO_COLOR24m or 4m$TERM24m in‐
         dicates colors are disabled.

         1mtrue0m
             Same as unset, except that 4m$NO_COLOR24m is ignored.

         1mfalse0m
             The output will be monochrome.

         "16", "256", "24bit"
             Always use the base 16 ANSI colors, 256 colors, or 24 bit color, respectively.

         "auto-16", "auto-256", "auto-24bit"
             Use  the given quantity of colours, subject to 4m$TERM24m, and what the console is connected
             to.

     4m$SYSTEMD_URLIFY0m
         The value must be a boolean. Controls whether clickable links should be  generated  in  the
         output  for terminal emulators supporting this. This can be specified to override the deci‐
         sion that 1msystemd 22mmakes based on 4m$TERM24m and other conditions.

4mTIMEOUT24m(1)                                  User Commands                                 4mTIMEOUT24m(1)

1mNAME0m
     timeout - run a command with a time limit

1mSYNOPSIS0m
     1mtimeout 22m[4mOPTION24m]... 4mDURATION24m 4mCOMMAND24m [4mARG24m]...

1mDESCRIPTION0m
     Start COMMAND, and kill it if still running after DURATION.

     Mandatory arguments to long options are mandatory for short options too.

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#timeout-f1m-f, --foreground22m8;;
            when  not  running  timeout directly from a shell prompt, allow COMMAND to read from the
            TTY and get TTY signals; in this mode, children of COMMAND will not be timed out

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#timeout-k1m-k, --kill-after=DURATION22m8;;
            also send a KILL signal if COMMAND is still running this long after the  initial  signal
            was sent

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#timeout-p1m-p, --preserve-status22m8;;
            exit with the same status as COMMAND, even when the command times out

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#timeout-s1m-s, --signal=SIGNAL22m8;;
            specify  the  signal to be sent on timeout; SIGNAL may be a name like 'HUP' or a number;
            see 'kill 1m-l22m' for a list of signals

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#timeout-v1m-v, --verbose22m8;;
            diagnose to standard error any signal sent upon timeout

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/timeout#timeout--help1m--help22m8;;
            display this help and exit

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/timeout#timeout--version1m--version22m8;;
            output version information and exit

     DURATION is a floating point number with an optional suffix: 's' for seconds (the default), 'm'
     for minutes, 'h' for hours or 'd' for days.  A duration of 0 disables the associated timeout.

     Upon timeout, send the TERM signal to COMMAND, if no other SIGNAL specified.  The  TERM  signal
     kills  any  process  that  does not block or catch that signal.  It may be necessary to use the
     KILL signal, since this signal can't be caught.

   1mExit status:0m
     124  if COMMAND times out, and 1m--preserve-status 22mis not specified
     125  if the timeout command itself fails
     126  if COMMAND is found but cannot be invoked
     127  if COMMAND cannot be found
     137  if COMMAND (or timeout itself) is sent the KILL (9) signal (128+9)
     -    the exit status of COMMAND otherwise

1mBUGS0m
     Some platforms don't currently support timeouts beyond the year 2038.

4mTOUCH24m(1)                                    User Commands                                   4mTOUCH24m(1)

1mNAME0m
     touch - create file, or change file timestamps

1mSYNOPSIS0m
     1mtouch 22m[4mOPTION24m]... 4mFILE24m...

1mDESCRIPTION0m
     Update the access and modification times of each FILE to the current time.

     A FILE argument that does not exist is created empty, unless 1m-c 22mor 1m-h 22mis supplied.

     A  FILE  argument  string of - is handled specially and causes touch to change the times of the
     file associated with standard output.

     Mandatory arguments to long options are mandatory for short options too.

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#touch-a1m-a22m8;;     change only the access time

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#touch-c1m-c, --no-create22m8;;
            do not create any files

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#touch-d1m-d, --date=STRING22m8;;
            parse STRING and use it instead of current time

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#touch-f1m-f22m8;;     (ignored)

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#touch-h1m-h, --no-dereference22m8;;
            affect each symbolic link instead of any referenced file; useful only  on  systems  that
            can change the timestamps of a symlink

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#touch-m1m-m22m8;;     change only the modification time

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#touch-r1m-r, --reference=FILE22m8;;
            use this file's times instead of current time

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#touch-t1m-t [[CC]YY]MMDDhhmm[.ss]22m8;;
            use  specified  time  instead of current time, with a date-time format that differs from
            1m-d22m's

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html#touch--time1m--time=WORD22m8;;
            specify which time to change: access time (1m-a22m): 'access', 'atime',  'use';  modification
            time (1m-m22m): 'modify', 'mtime'

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/touch#touch--help1m--help22m8;;
            display this help and exit

     8;;https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/touch#touch--version1m--version22m8;;
            output version information and exit

1mDATE STRING0m
     The  --date=STRING is a mostly free format human readable date string such as "Sun, 29 Feb 2004
     16:21:42 -0800" or "2004-02-29 16:21:42" or even "next Thursday".  A date  string  may  contain
     items  indicating  calendar  date, time of day, time zone, day of week, relative time, relative
     date, and numbers.  An empty string indicates the beginning of the day.  The date string format
     is more complex than is easily documented here but is fully described in  the  info  documenta‐
     tion.

4mTRACEPATH24m(8)                                   iputils                                  4mTRACEPATH24m(8)

1mNAME0m
     tracepath - traces path to a network host discovering MTU along this path

1mSYNOPSIS0m
     1mtracepath 22m[1m-422m] [1m-622m] [1m-n22m] [1m-b22m] [1m-l 4m22mpktlen24m] [1m-m 4m22mmax_hops24m] [1m-p 4m22mport24m] [1m-V22m] {destination}

1mDESCRIPTION0m
     It  traces  the  network  path to 4mdestination24m discovering MTU along this path. It uses UDP port
     4mport24m or some random port. It is similar to 1mtraceroute22m. However, it does not  require  superuser
     privileges and has no fancy options.

     1mtracepath  -6 22mis a good replacement for 1mtraceroute6 22mand classic example of application of Linux
     error queues. The situation with IPv4 is worse, because commercial IP  routers  do  not  return
     enough information in ICMP error messages. Probably, it will change, when they are updated. For
     now it uses Van Jacobson's trick, sweeping a range of UDP ports to maintain trace history.

1mOPTIONS0m
     1m-40m
         Use IPv4 only.

     1m-60m
         Use IPv6 only.

     1m-n0m
         Print primarily IP addresses numerically.

     1m-b0m
         Print both: Host names and IP addresses.

     1m-l0m
         Sets the initial packet length to 4mpktlen24m instead of 65535 for 1mIPv4 22mor 128000 for 1mIPv622m.

     1m-m0m
         Set maximum hops (or maximum TTLs) to 4mmax_hops24m instead of 30.

     1m-p0m
         Sets the initial destination port to use.

     1m-V0m
         Print version and exit.

1mOUTPUT0m
         root@mops:~ # tracepath -6 3ffe:2400:0:109::2
          1?: [LOCALHOST]                              pmtu 1500
          1:  dust.inr.ac.ru                   0.411ms
          2:  dust.inr.ac.ru        asymm  1   0.390ms pmtu 1480
          2:  3ffe:2400:0:109::2               463.514ms reached
              Resume: pmtu 1480 hops 2 back 2


     The first column shows the TTL of the probe, followed by colon. Usually the value of TTL is ob‐
     tained  from the reply from the network, but sometimes it does not contain the necessary infor‐
     mation and we have to guess it. In this case the number is followed by ?.

     The second column shows the network hop which replied to the probe. It is either the address of
     the router or the word [LOCALHOST], if the probe was not sent to the network.

     The rest of the line shows miscellaneous information about the path to the  corresponding  net‐
     work  hop. It contains the value of RTT, and additionally it can show Path MTU when it changes.
     If the path is asymmetric or the probe finishes before it reaches the prescribed hop, the  num‐
     ber  of  hops in return direction is shown next to the keyword "asymm". This information is not
     reliable, e.g. the third line shows asymmetry of 1. This is because the first probe with TTL of
     2 was rejected at the first hop due to Path MTU Discovery.

     The last line summarizes information about all the paths to the destination. It shows  detected
     Path  MTU,  amount  of  hops to the destination and our guess about the number of hops from the
     destination to us, which can be different when the path is asymmetric.

1mHANDLING ERRORS0m
     In case of errors 1mtracepath 22mprints short error code.  allbox tab(:); lB lB lB.  T{ Output T}:T{
     Code T}:T{ Meaning T} lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB lB  lB.
     T{  !A T}:T{ EACCES T}:T{ Communication administratively prohibited T} T{ !H T}:T{ EHOSTUNREACH
     T}:T{ Destination host unreachable T} T{ !N T}:T{ ENETUNREACH  T}:T{  Destination  network  un‐
     reachable T} T{ !P T}:T{ EPROTO T}:T{ Destination protocol unreachable T} T{ pmtu N T}:T{ EMSG‐
     SIZE  T}:T{  Message too long T} T{ reached T}:T{ ECONNREFUSED T}:T{ Connection refused T} T{
     T}:T{ ETIMEDOUT T}:T{ Connection timed out T} T{ NET ERROR N T}:T{   T}:T{ Any other error T}


1mSEE ALSO0m
     1mtraceroute22m(8), 1mtraceroute622m(8), 1mping22m(8).

1mAUTHOR0m
     1mtracepath 22mwas written by Alexey Kuznetsov <kuznet@ms2.inr.ac.ru>.

1mSECURITY0m
     No security issues.

     This lapidary deserves to be elaborated.  1mtracepath 22mis not a privileged program, unlike 1mtracer‐0m
     1moute22m, 1mping 22mand other beasts of their kind.  1mtracepath 22mmay  be  executed  by  everyone  who  has
     enough  access  to the network to send UDP datagrams to the desired destination using the given
     port.

1mAVAILABILITY0m
     1mtracepath 22mis part of 4miputils24m package.

4mUMOUNT24m(8)                               System Administration                              4mUMOUNT24m(8)

1mNAME0m
     umount - unmount filesystems

1mSYNOPSIS0m
     1mumount -a 22m[1m-dflnrv22m] [1m-t 4m22mfstype24m] [1m-O 4m22moption24m...]

     1mumount 22m[1m-dflnrv22m] {4mdirectory24m|4mdevice24m}

     1mumount -h22m|1m-V0m

1mDESCRIPTION0m
     The  1mumount  22mcommand detaches the mentioned filesystem(s) from the file hierarchy. A filesystem
     is specified by giving the directory where it has been mounted. Giving the  special  device  on
     which  the filesystem lives may also work, but is obsolete, mainly because it will fail in case
     this device was mounted on more than one directory.

     Note that a filesystem cannot be unmounted when it is 'busy' - for example, when there are open
     files on it, or when some process has its working directory there, or when a swap file on it is
     in use. The offending process could even be 1mumount 22mitself - it opens libc, and libc in its turn
     may open for example locale files. A lazy unmount avoids this problem,  but  it  may  introduce
     other issues. See 1m--lazy 22mdescription below.

1mOPTIONS0m
     1m-a22m, 1m--all0m
         All  of  the filesystems described in 4m/proc/self/mountinfo24m (or in deprecated 4m/etc/mtab24m) are
         unmounted, except the proc, devfs, devpts, sysfs, rpc_pipefs  and  nfsd  filesystems.  This
         list of the filesystems may be replaced by 1m--types 22mumount option.

     1m-A22m, 1m--all-targets0m
         Unmount  all  mountpoints  in the current mount namespace for the specified filesystem. The
         filesystem can be specified by one of the mountpoints or the device name (or  UUID,  etc.).
         When  this  option  is  used  together  with 1m--recursive22m, then all nested mounts within the
         filesystem are recursively unmounted. This  option  is  only  supported  on  systems  where
         4m/etc/mtab24m is a symlink to 4m/proc/mounts24m.

     1m-c22m, 1m--no-canonicalize0m
         Do  not  canonicalize paths. The paths canonicalization is based on 1mstat22m(2) and 1mreadlink22m(2)
         system calls. These system calls may hang in some cases (for example on NFS  if  server  is
         not available). The option has to be used with canonical path to the mount point.

         This option is silently ignored by 1mumount 22mfor non-root users.

         For  more  details  about  this option see the 1mmount22m(8) man page. Note that 1mumount 22mdoes not
         pass this option to the 1m/sbin/umount.4m22mtype24m helpers.

     1m-d22m, 1m--detach-loop0m
         When the unmounted device was a loop device, also free this loop device. This option is un‐
         necessary for devices initialized by 1mmount22m(8), in this case  "autoclear"  functionality  is
         enabled by default.

     1m--fake0m
         Causes  everything to be done except for the actual system call or umount helper execution;
         this 'fakes' unmounting the filesystem. It can be used to remove entries  from  the  depre‐
         cated 4m/etc/mtab24m that were unmounted earlier with the 1m-n 22moption.

     1m-f22m, 1m--force0m
         Force an unmount (in case of an unreachable NFS system).

         Note  that  this option does not guarantee that umount command does not hang. It’s strongly
         recommended to use absolute paths  without  symlinks  to  avoid  unwanted  1mreadlink22m(2)  and
         1mstat22m(2) system calls on unreachable NFS in 1mumount22m.

     1m-i22m, 1m--internal-only0m
         Do  not call the 1m/sbin/umount.4m22mfilesystem24m helper even if it exists. By default such a helper
         program is called if it exists.

     1m-l22m, 1m--lazy0m
         Lazy unmount. Detach the filesystem from the file hierarchy now, and clean  up  all  refer‐
         ences to this filesystem as soon as it is not busy anymore.

         A  system  reboot  would  be expected in near future if you’re going to use this option for
         network filesystem or local filesystem with submounts. The recommended use-case for  1mumount0m
         1m-l  22mis  to  prevent  hangs  on  shutdown due to an unreachable network share where a normal
         1mumount 22mwill hang due to a downed server or a network partition. Remounts of the share  will
         not be possible.

     1m-N22m, 1m--namespace 4m22mns0m
         Perform  1mumount 22min the mount namespace specified by 4mns24m. 4mns24m is either PID of process running
         in that namespace or special file representing that namespace.

         1mumount 22mswitches to the namespace when it reads 4m/etc/fstab24m, writes 4m/etc/mtab24m (or  writes  to
         4m/run/mount24m)  and  calls 1mumount22m(2) system call, otherwise it runs in the original namespace.
         It means that the target mount namespace does not have to contain any  libraries  or  other
         requirements necessary to execute 1mumount22m(2) command.

         See 1mmount_namespaces22m(7) for more information.

     1m-n22m, 1m--no-mtab0m
         Unmount without writing in 4m/etc/mtab24m.

     1m-O22m, 1m--test-opts 4m22moption24m...
         Unmount  only  the  filesystems that have the specified option set in 4m/etc/fstab24m. More than
         one option may be specified in a comma-separated list. Each option can be prefixed with  1mno0m
         to indicate that no action should be taken for this option.

     1m-q22m, 1m--quiet0m
         Suppress "not mounted" error messages.

     1m-R22m, 1m--recursive0m
         Recursively unmount each specified directory. Recursion for each directory will stop if any
         unmount  operation  in the chain fails for any reason. The relationship between mountpoints
         is determined by 4m/proc/self/mountinfo24m entries. The filesystem must be specified  by  mount‐
         point path; a recursive unmount by device name (or UUID) is unsupported. Since version 2.37
         it umounts also all over-mounted filesystems (more filesystems on the same mountpoint).

     1m-r22m, 1m--read-only0m
         When an unmount fails, try to remount the filesystem read-only.

     1m-t22m, 1m--types 4m22mtype24m...
         Indicate  that  the actions should only be taken on filesystems of the specified 4mtype24m. More
         than one type may be specified in a comma-separated list. The list of filesystem types  can
         be  prefixed  with  1mno  22mto indicate that no action should be taken for all of the mentioned
         types.  Note  that  1mumount  22mreads  information  about  mounted  filesystems   from   kernel
         (4m/proc/mounts24m)  and  filesystem  names  may  be different than filesystem names used in the
         4m/etc/fstab24m (e.g., "nfs4" vs. "nfs").

     1m-v22m, 1m--verbose0m
         Verbose mode.

     1m-h22m, 1m--help0m
         Display help text and exit.

     1m-V22m, 1m--version0m
         Display version and exit.

1mNON-SUPERUSER UMOUNTS0m
     Normally, only the superuser can umount filesystems. However, when 4mfstab24m contains the 1muser  22mop‐
     tion  on a line, anybody can umount the corresponding filesystem. For more details see 1mmount22m(8)
     man page.

     Since version 2.34 the 1mumount 22mcommand can be used to perform umount  operation  also  for  fuse
     filesystems  if kernel mount table contains user’s ID. In this case 4mfstab24m 1muser= 22mmount option is
     not required.

     Since version 2.35 1mumount 22mcommand does not exit when user permissions are inadequate by  inter‐
     nal  1mlibmount  22msecurity rules. It drops suid permissions and continue as regular non-root user.
     This can be used to support use-cases where root permissions  are  not  necessary  (e.g.,  fuse
     filesystems, user namespaces, etc).

1mLOOP DEVICE0m
     The  1mumount  22mcommand  will  automatically detach loop device previously initialized by 1mmount22m(8)
     command independently of 4m/etc/mtab24m.

     In this case the device is initialized with "autoclear" flag (see 1mlosetup22m(8)  output  for  more
     details),  otherwise  it’s necessary to use the option 1m--detach-loop 22mor call 1mlosetup -d 4m22mdevice24m.
     The autoclear feature is supported since Linux 2.6.25.

     Note that since Linux v3.7 kernel uses "lazy device destruction". The  system  just  marks  the
     loop device by autoclear flag and destroys it later. If you need to wait for a complete removal
     of the loop device, call 1mudevadm settle 22mafter 1mumount22m.

1mEXIT STATUS0m
     1mumount 22mhas the following exit status values (the bits can be ORed):

     1m00m
         success

     1m10m
         incorrect invocation or permissions

     1m20m
         system error (out of memory, cannot fork, no more loop devices)

     1m40m
         internal 1mmount 22mbug

     1m80m
         user interrupt

     1m160m
         problems writing or locking 4m/etc/mtab0m

     1m320m
         mount failure

     1m640m
         some umount succeeded

         The  command 1mumount -a 22mreturns 0 (all succeeded), 32 (all failed), or 64 (some failed, some
         succeeded).

     1m1260m
         failed to execute external /sbin/umount.<type> mount helper (since util-linux v2.41)

1mEXTERNAL HELPERS0m
     The syntax of external unmount helpers is:

        1mumount.4m22msuffix24m {4mdirectory24m|4mdevice24m} [1m-flnrv22m] [1m-N 4m22mnamespace24m] [1m-t 4m22mtype24m.4msubtype24m]

     where 4msuffix24m is the filesystem type (or the value from a 1muhelper= 22mor 1mhelper= 22mmarker in the mtab
     file). The 1m-t 22moption can be used for filesystems that have subtype support. For example:

        1mumount.fuse -t fuse.sshfs0m

     A 1muhelper=4m22msomething24m marker (unprivileged helper) can appear in the 4m/etc/mtab24m file when ordinary
     users need to be able to unmount a mountpoint that is not defined in  4m/etc/fstab24m  (for  example
     for a device that was mounted by 1mudisks22m(1)).

     A   1mhelper=4m22mtype24m   marker   in  the  4mmtab24m  file  will  redirect  all  unmount  requests  to  the
     1m/sbin/umount.4m22mtype24m helper independently of UID.

     Note that 4m/etc/mtab24m is currently deprecated and 1mhelper= 22mand other userspace mount  options  are
     maintained by 1mlibmount22m.

     The  exit status value of the helper is returned as the exit status of 1mumount22m(8). The value 126
     is used if the mount helper program is found, but the 1mexecl22m(3) failed.

1mENVIRONMENT0m
     1mLIBMOUNT_FSTAB22m=<path>
         overrides the default location of the 4mfstab24m file (ignored for 1msuid22m)

     1mLIBMOUNT_DEBUG22m=all
         enables 1mlibmount 22mdebug output

1mFILES0m
     4m/etc/mtab0m
         table of mounted filesystems (deprecated and usually replaced by symlink to 4m/proc/mounts24m)

     4m/etc/fstab0m
         table of known filesystems

     4m/proc/self/mountinfo0m
         table of mounted filesystems generated by kernel.

1mHISTORY0m
     A 1mumount 22mcommand appeared in Version 6 AT&T UNIX.

1mSEE ALSO0m
     1mumount22m(2), 1mlosetup22m(8), 1mmount_namespaces22m(7), 1mmount22m(8)

1mREPORTING BUGS0m
     For bug reports, use the 34missue tracker 0m<https://github.com/util-linux/util-linux/issues>.

1mAVAILABILITY0m
     The 1mumount 22mcommand is part of the util-linux package which can be downloaded from 34mLinux  Kernel0m
     34mArchive 0m<https://www.kernel.org/pub/linux/utils/util-linux/>.

util-linux 2.42.4                            2026-09-21                                    4mUMOUNT24m(8)

1mNAME0m
