unzip.text:
4mUNZIP24m(1L)                                                                                  4mUNZIP24m(1L)

1mNAME0m
     unzip - list, test and extract compressed files in a ZIP archive

1mSYNOPSIS0m
     1munzip   22m[1m-Z22m]  [1m-cflptTuvz22m[1mabjnoqsCDKLMUVWX$/:^22m]]  4mfile24m[4m.zip24m]  [4mfile(s)24m ...]   [1m-x 4m22mxfile(s)24m ...]
     [1m-d 4m22mexdir24m]

1mDESCRIPTION0m
     4munzip24m will list, test, or extract files from a ZIP archive, commonly found on  MS-DOS  systems.
     The  default behavior (with no options) is to extract into the current directory (and subdirec‐
     tories below it) all files from the specified ZIP archive.  A companion program, 4mzip24m(1L),  cre‐
     ates  ZIP  archives;  both  programs are compatible with archives created by PKWARE's 4mPKZIP24m and
     4mPKUNZIP24m for MS-DOS, but in many cases the program options or default behaviors differ.

1mARGUMENTS0m
     4mfile24m[4m.zip24m]
            Path of the ZIP archive(s).  If the file specification is a wildcard, each matching file
            is processed in an order determined by the operating system (or file system).  Only  the
            filename can be a wildcard; the path itself cannot.  Wildcard expressions are similar to
            those supported in commonly used Unix shells (4msh24m, 4mksh24m, 4mcsh24m) and may contain:

            *      matches a sequence of 0 or more characters

            ?      matches exactly 1 character

            [...]  matches any single character found inside the brackets; ranges are specified by a
                   beginning  character, a hyphen, and an ending character.  If an exclamation point
                   or a caret (‘!' or ‘^') follows the left bracket, then the  range  of  characters
                   within  the brackets is complemented (that is, anything 4mexcept24m the characters in‐
                   side the brackets is considered a match).  To specify a  verbatim  left  bracket,
                   the three-character sequence ‘‘[[]'' has to be used.

            (Be  sure  to quote any character that might otherwise be interpreted or modified by the
            operating system, particularly under Unix and VMS.)  If no matches are found, the speci‐
            fication is assumed to be a literal filename; and if that also fails, the suffix .zip is
            appended.  Note that self-extracting ZIP files are supported,  as  with  any  other  ZIP
            archive; just specify the .exe suffix (if any) explicitly.

     [4mfile(s)24m]
            An optional list of archive members to be processed, separated by spaces.  (VMS versions
            compiled  with VMSCLI defined must delimit files with commas instead.  See 1m-v 22min 1mOPTIONS0m
            below.)  Regular expressions (wildcards) may be used  to  match  multiple  members;  see
            above.  Again, be sure to quote expressions that would otherwise be expanded or modified
            by the operating system.

     [1m-x 4m22mxfile(s)24m]
            An  optional  list  of  archive  members to be excluded from processing.  Since wildcard
            characters normally match (‘/') directory separators (for exceptions see the option 1m-W22m),
            this option may be used to exclude any files that are in subdirectories.   For  example,
            ‘‘unzip  foo *.[ch] -x */*'' would extract all C source files in the main directory, but
            none in any subdirectories.  Without the 1m-x 22moption, all C source files in  all  directo‐
            ries within the zipfile would be extracted.

     [1m-d 4m22mexdir24m]
            An  optional directory to which to extract files.  By default, all files and subdirecto‐
            ries are recreated in the current directory; the 1m-d 22moption allows extraction in an arbi‐
            trary directory (always assuming one has permission to write to  the  directory).   This
            option  need  not  appear at the end of the command line; it is also accepted before the
            zipfile specification (with the normal options), immediately after the zipfile  specifi‐
            cation,  or between the 4mfile(s)24m and the 1m-x 22moption.  The option and directory may be con‐
            catenated without any white space between them, but note  that  this  may  cause  normal
            shell  behavior to be suppressed.  In particular, ‘‘-d ~'' (tilde) is expanded by Unix C
            shells into the name of the user's home directory, but ‘‘-d~'' is treated as  a  literal
            subdirectory ‘‘1m~22m'' of the current directory.

1mOPTIONS0m
     Note  that,  in order to support obsolescent hardware, 4munzip24m's usage screen is limited to 22 or
     23 lines and should therefore be considered only a reminder of the basic  4munzip24m  syntax  rather
     than an exhaustive list of all possible flags.  The exhaustive list follows:

     1m-Z     4m22mzipinfo24m(1L)  mode.  If the first option on the command line is 1m-Z22m, the remaining options
            are taken to be 4mzipinfo24m(1L) options.  See the appropriate manual page for a  description
            of these options.

     1m-A     22m[OS/2, Unix DLL] print extended help for the DLL's programming interface (API).

     1m-c     22mextract  files  to stdout/screen (‘‘CRT'').  This option is similar to the 1m-p 22moption ex‐
            cept that the name of each file is printed as it is extracted, the 1m-a 22moption is allowed,
            and ASCII-EBCDIC conversion is automatically performed if appropriate.  This  option  is
            not listed in the 4munzip24m usage screen.

     1m-f     22mfreshen  existing  files,  i.e., extract only those files that already exist on disk and
            that are newer than the disk copies.  By default 4munzip24m queries before  overwriting,  but
            the  1m-o 22moption may be used to suppress the queries.  Note that under many operating sys‐
            tems, the TZ (timezone) environment variable must be set correctly in order for  1m-f  22mand
            1m-u 22mto work properly (under Unix the variable is usually set automatically).  The reasons
            for this are somewhat subtle but have to do with the differences between DOS-format file
            times (always local time) and Unix-format times (always in GMT/UTC) and the necessity to
            compare  the two.  A typical TZ value is ‘‘PST8PDT'' (US Pacific time with automatic ad‐
            justment for Daylight Savings Time or ‘‘summer time'').

     1m-l     22mlist archive files (short format).  The names, uncompressed file sizes and  modification
            dates  and  times  of  the  specified files are printed, along with totals for all files
            specified.  If UnZip was compiled with OS2_EAS defined, the 1m-l 22moption also lists columns
            for the sizes of stored OS/2 extended attributes (EAs) and  OS/2  access  control  lists
            (ACLs).  In addition, the zipfile comment and individual file comments (if any) are dis‐
            played.  If a file was archived from a single-case file system (for example, the old MS-
            DOS FAT file system) and the 1m-L 22moption was given, the filename is converted to lowercase
            and is prefixed with a caret (^).

     1m-p     22mextract  files  to  pipe (stdout).  Nothing but the file data is sent to stdout, and the
            files are always extracted in binary format, just as they are stored (no conversions).

     1m-t     22mtest archive files.  This option extracts each specified file in memory and compares the
            CRC (cyclic redundancy check, an enhanced checksum) of the expanded file with the origi‐
            nal file's stored CRC value.

     1m-T     22m[most OSes] set the timestamp on the archive(s) to that of the newest file in each  one.
            This  corresponds  to  4mzip24m's  1m-go 22moption except that it can be used on wildcard zipfiles
            (e.g., ‘‘unzip -T \*.zip'') and is much faster.

     1m-u     22mupdate existing files and create new ones if needed.   This  option  performs  the  same
            function  as the 1m-f 22moption, extracting (with query) files that are newer than those with
            the same name on disk, and in addition it extracts those files that do not already exist
            on disk.  See 1m-f 22mabove for information on setting the timezone properly.

     1m-v     22mlist archive files (verbose format) or show diagnostic version info.   This  option  has
            evolved  and now behaves as both an option and a modifier.  As an option it has two pur‐
            poses:  when a zipfile is specified with no other options, 1m-v 22mlists archive  files  ver‐
            bosely, adding to the basic 1m-l 22minfo the compression method, compressed size, compression
            ratio and 32-bit CRC.  In contrast to most of the competing utilities, 4munzip24m removes the
            12  additional  header  bytes  of  encrypted  entries  from the compressed size numbers.
            Therefore, compressed size and compression ratio figures are independent of the  entry's
            encryption  status  and show the correct compression performance.  (The complete size of
            the encrypted compressed data stream for zipfile entries is reported by the more verbose
            4mzipinfo24m(1L) reports, see the separate manual.)  When no zipfile is specified  (that  is,
            the  complete command is simply ‘‘unzip -v''), a diagnostic screen is printed.  In addi‐
            tion to the normal header with release date and version, 4munzip24m lists the  home  Info-ZIP
            ftp  site  and where to find a list of other ftp and non-ftp sites; the target operating
            system for which it was compiled, as well as (possibly) the hardware  on  which  it  was
            compiled,  the compiler and version used, and the compilation date; any special compila‐
            tion options that might affect the program's operation (see also 1mDECRYPTION 22mbelow);  and
            any  options stored in environment variables that might do the same (see 1mENVIRONMENT OP‐0m
            1mTIONS 22mbelow).  As a modifier it works in conjunction with other options  (e.g.,  1m-t22m)  to
            produce  more verbose or debugging output; this is not yet fully implemented but will be
            in future releases.

     1m-z     22mdisplay only the archive comment.

1mMODIFIERS0m
     1m-a     22mconvert text files.  Ordinarily all files are extracted exactly as they are  stored  (as
            ‘‘binary''  files).   The  1m-a 22moption causes files identified by 4mzip24m as text files (those
            with the ‘t' label in 4mzipinfo24m listings, rather than ‘b') to be  automatically  extracted
            as such, converting line endings, end-of-file characters and the character set itself as
            necessary.  (For example, Unix files use line feeds (LFs) for end-of-line (EOL) and have
            no  end-of-file  (EOF) marker; Macintoshes use carriage returns (CRs) for EOLs; and most
            PC operating systems use CR+LF for EOLs and control-Z for EOF.  In addition,  IBM  main‐
            frames  and  the  Michigan  Terminal System use EBCDIC rather than the more common ASCII
            character set, and NT supports Unicode.)  Note that 4mzip24m's identification of  text  files
            is  by no means perfect; some ‘‘text'' files may actually be binary and vice versa.  4mun‐0m
            4mzip24m therefore prints ‘‘[text]'' or ‘‘[binary]'' as a visual check for each file  it  ex‐
            tracts  when  using  the  1m-a 22moption.  The 1m-aa 22moption forces all files to be extracted as
            text, regardless of the supposed file type.  On VMS, see also 1m-S22m.

     1m-b     22m[general] treat all files as binary (no text conversions).  This is a shortcut for 1m---a22m.

     1m-b     22m[Tandem] force the creation files with filecode type 180 ('C') when extracting  Zip  en‐
            tries marked as "text". (On Tandem, 1m-a 22mis enabled by default, see above).

     1m-b     22m[VMS]  auto-convert binary files (see 1m-a 22mabove) to fixed-length, 512-byte record format.
            Doubling the option (1m-bb22m) forces all files to be extracted in this format. When extract‐
            ing to standard output (1m-c 22mor 1m-p 22moption in  effect),  the  default  conversion  of  text
            record delimiters is disabled for binary (1m-b22m) resp. all (1m-bb22m) files.

     1m-B     22m[when compiled with UNIXBACKUP defined] save a backup copy of each overwritten file. The
            backup file is gets the name of the target file with a tilde and optionally a unique se‐
            quence  number  (up  to 5 digits) appended.  The sequence number is applied whenever an‐
            other file with the original name plus tilde already exists.  When  used  together  with
            the  "overwrite  all"  option 1m-o22m, numbered backup files are never created. In this case,
            all backup files are named as the original file with an appended tilde, existing  backup
            files  are deleted without notice.  This feature works similarly to the default behavior
            of 4memacs24m(1) in many locations.

            Example: the old copy of ‘‘foo'' is renamed to ‘‘foo~''.

            Warning: Users should be aware that the 1m-B 22moption does not prevent loss of existing data
            under all circumstances.  For example, when 4munzip24m is run in overwrite-all mode,  an  ex‐
            isting  ‘‘foo~''  file  is  deleted before 4munzip24m attempts to rename ‘‘foo'' to ‘‘foo~''.
            When this rename attempt fails (because of a file  locks,  insufficient  privileges,  or
            ...),  the  extraction  of  ‘‘foo~''  gets cancelled, but the old backup file is already
            lost.  A similar scenario takes place when the sequence number range for numbered backup
            files gets exhausted (99999, or 65535 for 16-bit systems).  In  this  case,  the  backup
            file  with the maximum sequence number is deleted and replaced by the new backup version
            without notice.

     1m-C     22muse case-insensitive matching for the selection of archive entries from the command-line
            list of extract selection patterns.  4munzip24m's philosophy is ‘‘you get what you ask  for''
            (this  is  also  responsible for the 1m-L22m/1m-U 22mchange; see the relevant options below).  Be‐
            cause some file systems are fully case-sensitive (notably those under the Unix operating
            system) and because both ZIP archives and 4munzip24m itself are  portable  across  platforms,
            4munzip24m's  default  behavior  is  to match both wildcard and literal filenames case-sensi‐
            tively.  That is, specifying ‘‘makefile'' on the command line will  4monly24m  match  ‘‘make‐
            file''  in  the  archive,  not  ‘‘Makefile'' or ‘‘MAKEFILE'' (and similarly for wildcard
            specifications).  Since this does not correspond to the behavior of many  other  operat‐
            ing/file  systems  (for example, OS/2 HPFS, which preserves mixed case but is not sensi‐
            tive to it), the 1m-C 22moption may be used to force all filename matches to be case-insensi‐
            tive.  In the  example  above,  all  three  files  would  then  match  ‘‘makefile''  (or
            ‘‘make*'',  or  similar).  The 1m-C 22moption affects file specs in both the normal file list
            and the excluded-file list (xlist).

            matching of archive entries to existing files on the extraction path.  On a  case-sensi‐

1mENVIRONMENT OPTIONS0m
     4munzip24m's  default  behavior may be modified via options placed in an environment variable.  This
     can be done with any option, but it is probably most useful with the 1m-a22m, 1m-L22m, 1m-C22m, 1m-q22m, 1m-o22m, or  1m-n0m
     modifiers:   make  4munzip24m auto-convert text files by default, make it convert filenames from up‐
     percase systems to lowercase, make it match names case-insensitively, make it quieter, or  make
     it  always  overwrite or never overwrite files as it extracts them.  For example, to make 4munzip0m
     act as quietly as possible, only reporting errors, one would use one of the following commands:

       Unix Bourne shell:
            UNZIP=-qq; export UNZIP

       Unix C shell:
            setenv UNZIP -qq

       OS/2 or MS-DOS:
            set UNZIP=-qq

       VMS (quotes for 4mlowercase24m):
            define UNZIP_OPTS "-qq"

     Environment options are, in effect, considered to be just like any other command-line  options,
     except  that  they are effectively the first options on the command line.  To override an envi‐
     ronment option, one may use the ‘‘minus operator'' to remove it.  For instance, to override one
     of the quiet-flags in the example above, use the command

     unzip --q[4mother24m 4moptions24m] zipfile

     The first hyphen is the normal switch character, and the second is a minus sign, acting on  the
     q  option.   Thus  the effect here is to cancel one quantum of quietness.  To cancel both quiet
     flags, two (or more) minuses may be used:

     unzip -t--q zipfile
     unzip ---qt zipfile

     (the two are equivalent).  This may seem awkward or confusing, but it is reasonably  intuitive:
     just  ignore  the  first  hyphen and go from there.  It is also consistent with the behavior of
     Unix 4mnice24m(1).

     As suggested by the examples above, the default variable names are UNZIP_OPTS  for  VMS  (where
     the  symbol used to install 4munzip24m as a foreign command would otherwise be confused with the en‐
     vironment variable), and UNZIP  for  all  other  operating  systems.   For  compatibility  with
     4mzip24m(1L),  UNZIPOPT  is also accepted (don't ask).  If both UNZIP and UNZIPOPT are defined, how‐
     ever, UNZIP takes precedence.  4munzip24m's diagnostic option (1m-v 22mwith no zipfile name) can be  used
     to check the values of all four possible 4munzip24m and 4mzipinfo24m environment variables.

     The  timezone  variable  (TZ) should be set according to the local timezone in order for the 1m-f0m
     and 1m-u 22mto operate correctly.  See the description of 1m-f 22mabove for details.  This  variable  may
     also  be  necessary  to  get  timestamps  of  extracted  files  to be set correctly.  The WIN32
     (Win9x/ME/NT4/2K/XP/2K3) port of 4munzip24m gets the timezone configuration from the  registry,  as‐
     suming it is correctly set in the Control Panel.  The TZ variable is ignored for this port.

1mDECRYPTION0m
     Encrypted  archives  are  fully supported by Info-ZIP software, but due to United States export
     restrictions, de-/encryption support might be disabled in your compiled binary.  However, since
     spring 2000, US export restrictions have been liberated, and our source archives do now include
     full crypt code.  In case you need binary distributions with crypt  support  enabled,  see  the
     file ‘‘WHERE'' in any Info-ZIP source or binary distribution for locations both inside and out‐
     side the US.

     Some  compiled versions of 4munzip24m may not support decryption.  To check a version for crypt sup‐
     port, either attempt to test or extract an encrypted archive, or else check 4munzip24m's  diagnostic
     screen  (see  the  1m-v  22moption above) for ‘‘[decryption]'' as one of the special compilation op‐
     tions.

     As noted above, the 1m-P 22moption may be used to supply a password on the command line,  but  at  a
     cost  in security.  The preferred decryption method is simply to extract normally; if a zipfile
     member is encrypted, 4munzip24m will prompt for the password without echoing what is  typed.   4munzip0m
     continues  to  use  the  same  password as long as it appears to be valid, by testing a 12-byte
     header on each file.  The correct password will always check out against the header, but  there
     is  a  1-in-256 chance that an incorrect password will as well.  (This is a security feature of
     the PKWARE zipfile format; it helps prevent brute-force attacks that  might  otherwise  gain  a
     large  speed  advantage by testing only the header.)  In the case that an incorrect password is
     given but it passes the header test anyway, either an incorrect CRC will be generated  for  the
     extracted data or else 4munzip24m will fail during the extraction because the ‘‘decrypted'' bytes do
     not constitute a valid compressed data stream.

     If  the first password fails the header check on some file, 4munzip24m will prompt for another pass‐
     word, and so on until all files are extracted.  If a password is not  known,  entering  a  null
     password  (that  is, just a carriage return or ‘‘Enter'') is taken as a signal to skip all fur‐
     ther prompting.  Only unencrypted files in the archive(s) will thereafter  be  extracted.   (In
     fact, that's not quite true; older versions of 4mzip24m(1L) and 4mzipcloak24m(1L) allowed null passwords,
     so  4munzip24m  checks  each  encrypted  file to see if the null password works.  This may result in
     ‘‘false positives'' and extraction errors, as noted above.)

     Archives encrypted with 8-bit passwords (for example, passwords with accented European  charac‐
     ters)  may  not be portable across systems and/or other archivers.  This problem stems from the
     use of multiple encoding methods for such characters, including Latin-1 (ISO  8859-1)  and  OEM
     code page 850.  DOS 4mPKZIP24m 2.04g uses the OEM code page; Windows 4mPKZIP24m 2.50 uses Latin-1 (and is
     therefore incompatible with DOS 4mPKZIP24m); Info-ZIP uses the OEM code page on DOS, OS/2 and Win3.x
     ports  but  ISO coding (Latin-1 etc.) everywhere else; and Nico Mak's 4mWinZip24m 6.x does not allow
     8-bit passwords at all.  4mUnZip24m 5.3 (or newer) attempts to use the default character  set  first
     (e.g.,  Latin-1),  followed  by  the alternate one (e.g., OEM code page) to test passwords.  On
     EBCDIC systems, if both of these fail, EBCDIC  encoding  will  be  tested  as  a  last  resort.
     (EBCDIC  is not tested on non-EBCDIC systems, because there are no known archivers that encrypt
     using EBCDIC encoding.)  ISO character encodings other than Latin-1 are not supported.  The new
     addition of (partially) Unicode (resp.  UTF-8) support in 4mUnZip24m 6.0 has not yet been adapted to
     the encryption password handling in 4munzip24m.  On systems that use UTF-8 as native  character  en‐
     coding,  4munzip24m simply tries decryption with the native UTF-8 encoded password; the built-in at‐
     tempts to check the password in translated encoding have not yet been adapted for UTF-8 support
     and will consequently fail.

1mEXAMPLES0m
     To use 4munzip24m to extract all members of the archive 4mletters.zip24m into the current  directory  and
     subdirectories below it, creating any subdirectories as necessary:

     unzip letters

     To extract all members of 4mletters.zip24m into the current directory only:

     unzip -j letters

     To  test  4mletters.zip24m,  printing only a summary message indicating whether the archive is OK or
     not:

     unzip -tq letters

     To test 4mall24m zipfiles in the current directory, printing only the summaries:

     unzip -tq \*.zip

     (The backslash before the asterisk is only required if the shell expands wildcards, as in Unix;
     double quotes could have been used instead, as in the source examples  below.)  To  extract  to
     standard  output all members of 4mletters.zip24m whose names end in 4m.tex24m, auto-converting to the lo‐
     cal end-of-line convention and piping the output into 4mmore24m(1):

     unzip -ca letters \*.tex | more

     To extract the binary file 4mpaper1.dvi24m to standard output and pipe it to a printing program:

     unzip -p articles paper1.dvi | dvips

     To extract all FORTRAN and C source files--*.f, *.c, *.h, and Makefile--into  the  /tmp  direc‐
     tory:

     unzip source.zip "*.[fch]" Makefile -d /tmp

     (the  double  quotes are necessary only in Unix and only if globbing is turned on).  To extract
     all FORTRAN and C source files, regardless of case (e.g., both *.c and *.C, and  any  makefile,
     Makefile, MAKEFILE or similar):

     unzip -C source.zip "*.[fch]" makefile -d /tmp

     To  extract  any such files but convert any uppercase MS-DOS or VMS names to lowercase and con‐
     vert the line-endings of all of the files to the local standard (without respect to  any  files
     that might be marked ‘‘binary''):

     unzip -aaCL source.zip "*.[fch]" makefile -d /tmp

     To  extract only newer versions of the files already in the current directory, without querying
     (NOTE:  be careful of unzipping in one timezone a  zipfile  created  in  another--ZIP  archives
     other  than  those created by Zip 2.1 or later contain no timezone information, and a ‘‘newer''
     file from an eastern timezone may, in fact, be older):

     unzip -fo sources

     To extract newer versions of the files already in the current directory and to create any files
     not already there (same caveat as previous example):

     unzip -uo sources

     To display a diagnostic screen showing which 4munzip24m and 4mzipinfo24m options are stored  in  environ‐
     ment  variables,  whether decryption support was compiled in, the compiler with which 4munzip24m was
     compiled, etc.:

     unzip -v

     In the last five examples, assume that UNZIP or UNZIP_OPTS is set to -q.  To do a singly  quiet
     listing:

     unzip -l file.zip

     To do a doubly quiet listing:

     unzip -ql file.zip

     (Note that the ‘‘.zip'' is generally not necessary.)  To do a standard listing:

     unzip --ql file.zip
     or
     unzip -l-q file.zip
     or
     unzip -l--q file.zip
     (Extra minuses in options don't hurt.)

1mTIPS0m
     The  current  maintainer,  being a lazy sort, finds it very useful to define a pair of aliases:
     tt for ‘‘unzip -tq'' and ii for ‘‘unzip -Z'' (or ‘‘zipinfo'').  One may then simply  type  ‘‘tt
     zipfile'' to test an archive, something that is worth making a habit of doing.  With luck 4munzip0m
     will  report  ‘‘No  errors  detected  in  compressed data of zipfile.zip,'' after which one may
     breathe a sigh of relief.

     The maintainer also finds it useful to set the UNZIP environment variable  to  ‘‘-aL''  and  is
     tempted to add ‘‘-C'' as well.  His ZIPINFO variable is set to ‘‘-z''.

1mDIAGNOSTICS0m
     The exit status (or error level) approximates the exit codes defined by PKWARE and takes on the
     following values, except under VMS:

            0      normal; no errors or warnings detected.

            1      one  or  more  warning errors were encountered, but processing completed success‐
                   fully anyway.  This includes zipfiles where one or more files was skipped due  to
                   unsupported compression method or encryption with an unknown password.

            2      a  generic  error  in  the zipfile format was detected.  Processing may have com‐
                   pleted successfully anyway; some broken zipfiles created by other archivers  have
                   simple work-arounds.

            3      a  severe  error  in the zipfile format was detected.  Processing probably failed
                   immediately.

            4      4munzip24m was unable to allocate memory for one or more buffers during  program  ini‐
                   tialization.

            5      4munzip24m was unable to allocate memory or unable to obtain a tty to read the decryp‐
                   tion password(s).

            6      4munzip24m was unable to allocate memory during decompression to disk.

            7      4munzip24m was unable to allocate memory during in-memory decompression.

            8      [currently not used]

            9      the specified zipfiles were not found.

            10     invalid options were specified on the command line.

            11     no matching files were found.

            12     invalid  zip  file  with  overlapped components (possible zip-bomb). The zip-bomb
                   checks can be disabled by using the UNZIP_DISABLE_ZIPBOMB_DETECTION=TRUE environ‐
                   ment variable.

            50     the disk is (or was) full during extraction.

            51     the end of the ZIP archive was encountered prematurely.

            80     the user aborted 4munzip24m prematurely with control-C (or similar)

            81     testing or extraction of one or more files failed due to unsupported  compression
                   methods or unsupported decryption.

            82     no files were found due to bad decryption password(s).  (If even one file is suc‐
                   cessfully processed, however, the exit status is 1.)

     VMS  interprets  standard Unix (or PC) return values as other, scarier-looking things, so 4munzip0m
     instead maps them into VMS-style status codes.  The current mapping is as  follows:    1  (suc‐
     cess)  for  normal  exit,  0x7fff0001  for  warning  errors,  and  (0x7fff000?  + 16*normal_un‐
     zip_exit_status) for all other errors, where the ‘?' is 2 (error) for 4munzip24m values 2, 9-11  and
     80-82,  and 4 (fatal error) for the remaining ones (3-8, 50, 51).  In addition, there is a com‐
     pilation option to expand upon this behavior:  defining RETURN_CODES results in  a  human-read‐
     able explanation of what the error status means.

1mBUGS0m
     Multi-part  archives are not yet supported, except in conjunction with 4mzip24m.  (All parts must be
     concatenated together in order, and then ‘‘zip -F'' (for 4mzip24m 4m2.x24m) or ‘‘zip -FF'' (for 4mzip24m  4m3.x24m)
     must  be performed on the concatenated archive in order to ‘‘fix'' it.  Also, 4mzip24m 4m3.024m and later
     can combine multi-part (split) archives into a combined single-file  archive  using  ‘‘zip  -s-
     inarchive  -O  outarchive''.  See the 4mzip24m 4m324m manual page for more information.)  This will defi‐
     nitely be corrected in the next major release.

     Archives read from standard input are not yet supported, except with 4mfunzip24m (and then only  the
     first member of the archive can be extracted).

     Archives encrypted with 8-bit passwords (e.g., passwords with accented European characters) may
     not be portable across systems and/or other archivers.  See the discussion in 1mDECRYPTION 22mabove.

     4munzip24m's  1m-M 22m(‘‘more'') option tries to take into account automatic wrapping of long lines. How‐
     ever, the code may fail to detect the correct wrapping locations. First,  TAB  characters  (and
     similar  control  sequences) are not taken into account, they are handled as ordinary printable
     characters.  Second, depending on the actual system / OS port, 4munzip24m may not  detect  the  true
     screen geometry but rather rely on "commonly used" default dimensions.  The correct handling of
     tabs  would  require the implementation of a query for the actual tabulator setup on the output
     console.

     Dates, times and permissions of stored directories are not restored except under Unix. (On Win‐
     dows NT and successors, timestamps are now restored.)

     [MS-DOS] When extracting or testing files from an archive on a defective  floppy  diskette,  if
     the ‘‘Fail'' option is chosen from DOS's ‘‘Abort, Retry, Fail?'' message, older versions of 4mun‐0m
     4mzip24m  may  hang the system, requiring a reboot.  This problem appears to be fixed, but control-C
     (or control-Break) can still be used to terminate 4munzip24m.

     Under DEC Ultrix, 4munzip24m would sometimes fail on long  zipfiles  (bad  CRC,  not  always  repro‐
     ducible).  This was apparently due either to a hardware bug (cache memory) or an operating sys‐
     tem bug (improper handling of page faults?).  Since Ultrix has been abandoned in favor of Digi‐
     tal Unix (OSF/1), this may not be an issue anymore.

     [Unix]  Unix  special files such as FIFO buffers (named pipes), block devices and character de‐
     vices are not restored even if they are somehow represented in the zipfile, nor are hard-linked
     files relinked.  Basically the only file types restored by 4munzip24m are regular files, directories
     and symbolic (soft) links.

     [OS/2] Extended attributes for existing directories are only updated  if  the  1m-o  22m(‘‘overwrite
     all'') option is given.  This is a limitation of the operating system; because directories only
     have a creation time associated with them, 4munzip24m has no way to determine whether the stored at‐
     tributes  are newer or older than those on disk.  In practice this may mean a two-pass approach
     is required:  first unpack the archive normally (with or without  freshening/updating  existing
     files), then overwrite just the directory entries (e.g., ‘‘unzip -o foo */'').

     [VMS]  When  extracting to another directory, only the 4m[.foo]24m syntax is accepted for the 1m-d 22mop‐
     tion; the simple Unix 4mfoo24m syntax is silently ignored (as is the less common  VMS  4mfoo.dir24m  syn‐
     tax).

     [VMS]  When  the file being extracted already exists, 4munzip24m's query only allows skipping, over‐
     writing or renaming; there should additionally be a choice for creating a new  version  of  the
     file.   In  fact,  the  ‘‘overwrite''  choice does create a new version; the old version is not
     overwritten or deleted.

1mSEE ALSO0m
     4mfunzip24m(1L), 4mzip24m(1L), 4mzipcloak24m(1L), 4mzipgrep24m(1L), 4mzipinfo24m(1L), 4mzipnote24m(1L), 4mzipsplit24m(1L)

     Gordon  (Zip, general maintenance, shared code, Zip64, Win32, Unix, Unicode); Christian Spieler
     (UnZip maintenance coordination, VMS, MS-DOS, Win32, shared code, general Zip and  UnZip  inte‐

     DLLs); Kai Uwe Rommel (OS/2, Win32); Steven M. Schweda (VMS, Unix, support  of  new  features);

uptime.text:
4mUPTIME24m(1)                              General Commands Manual                             4mUPTIME24m(1)

1mNAME0m
     uptime - Tell how long the system has been running.

1mSYNOPSIS0m
     1muptime 22m[4moption24m ...]

1mDESCRIPTION0m
     1muptime  22mgives  a one line display of the following information.  The current time, how long the
     system has been running, how many users are currently logged on, and the system  load  averages
     for the past 1, 5, and 15 minutes.

     This is the same information contained in the header line displayed by 1mw22m(1).

     System  load averages is the average number of processes that are either in a runnable or unin‐
     terruptible state.  A process in a runnable state is either using the CPU or waiting to use the
     CPU.  A process in uninterruptible state is waiting for some I/O access, eg waiting  for  disk.
     The averages are taken over the three time intervals.  Load averages are not normalized for the
     number  of CPUs in a system, so a load average of 1 means a single CPU system is loaded all the
     time while on a 4 CPU system it means it was idle 75% of the time.

1mOPTIONS0m
     1m-c22m, 1m--container0m
            show the container uptime instead of system uptime.

     1m-p22m, 1m--pretty0m
            show uptime in pretty format

     1m-h22m, 1m--help0m
            display this help text

     1m-r22m, 1m--raw0m
            Display values in a raw format. Current time and uptime are displayed in seconds.

     1m-s22m, 1m--since0m
            system up since, in yyyy-mm-dd HH:MM:SS format

     1m-V22m, 1m--version0m
            display version information and exit

1mENVIRONMENT0m
     1mPROCPS_CONTAINER0m
            If $1mPROCPS_CONTAINER 22mis set, then 1muptime 22mbehaves as if the 1m--container 22moption  has  been
            given.

1mFILES0m
     4m/var/run/utmp0m
            information about who is currently logged on

     4m/proc24m  process information

1mSEE ALSO0m
     1mps22m(1), 1mtop22m(1), 1mutmp22m(5), 1mw22m(1)

1mREPORTING BUGS0m
     Please send bug reports to 8;;mailto:procps@freelists.orgprocps@freelists.org8;;.

userdel.text:
4mUSERDEL24m(8)                           System Management Commands                           4mUSERDEL24m(8)

1mNAME0m
     userdel - delete a user account and related files

1mSYNOPSIS0m
     1muserdel 22m[options] 4mLOGIN0m

1mDESCRIPTION0m
     The  1muserdel  22mcommand modifies the system account files, deleting all entries that refer to the
     user name 4mLOGIN24m. The named user must exist.

1mOPTIONS0m
     The options which apply to the 1muserdel 22mcommand are:

     1m-f22m, 1m--force0m
         This option forces the removal of the user account and any other requested  actions,  skip‐
         ping any safety checks.

         4mNote:24m This option is dangerous and may leave your system in an inconsistent state.

     1m-h22m, 1m--help0m
         Display help message and exit.

     1m-r22m, 1m--remove0m
         Files in the user's home directory will be removed along with the home directory itself and
         the user's mail spool. Files located in other file systems will have to be searched for and
         deleted manually.

         The mail spool is defined by the 1mMAIL_DIR 22mvariable in the login.defs file.

     1m-R22m, 1m--root 4m22mCHROOT_DIR0m
         Apply  changes  in  the  4mCHROOT_DIR24m  directory and use the configuration files from the 4mCH‐0m
         4mROOT_DIR24m directory. Only absolute paths are supported. No SELINUX support.

     1m-P22m, 1m--prefix 4m22mPREFIX_DIR0m
         Apply changes in the 4mPREFIX_DIR24m directory and use the configuration  files  from  the  4mPRE‐0m
         4mFIX_DIR24m directory. This option does not chroot and is intended for preparing a cross-compi‐
         lation  target. Some limitations: NIS and LDAP users/groups are not verified. PAM authenti‐
         cation is using the host files. No SELINUX support.

     1m-Z22m, 1m--selinux-user0m
         Remove any SELinux user mapping for the user's login.

1mCONFIGURATION0m
     The following configuration variables in /etc/login.defs change the behavior of this tool:

     1mMAIL_DIR 22m(string)
         The mail spool directory. This is needed to manipulate the mailbox when  its  corresponding
         user  account is modified or deleted. If not specified, a compile-time default is used. The
         parameter CREATE_MAIL_SPOOL in  /etc/default/useradd  determines  whether  the  mail  spool
         should be created.

     1mMAIL_FILE 22m(string)
         Defines the location of the users mail spool files relatively to their home directory.

     The 1mMAIL_DIR 22mand 1mMAIL_FILE 22mvariables are used by 1museradd22m, 1musermod22m, and 1muserdel 22mto create, move,
     or delete the user's mail spool.

     1mMAX_MEMBERS_PER_GROUP 22m(number)
         Maximum  members  per group entry. When the maximum is reached, a new group entry (line) is
         started in /etc/group (with the same name, same password, and same GID).

         The default value is 0, meaning that there are no limits in the  number  of  members  in  a
         group.

         This  feature (split group) permits to limit the length of lines in the group file. This is
         useful to make sure that lines for NIS groups are not larger than 1024 characters.

         If you need to enforce such limit, you can use 25.

         Note: split groups may not be supported by all tools (even in the  Shadow  toolsuite).  You
         should not use this variable unless you really need it.

     1mUSERDEL_CMD 22m(string)
         If  defined,  this  command is run when removing a user. It should remove any at/cron/print
         jobs etc. owned by the user to be removed (passed as the first argument).

         The return code of the script is not taken into account.

         Here is an example script, which removes the user's cron, at and print jobs:

             #! /bin/sh

             # Check for the required argument.
             if [ $# != 1 ]; then
                  echo "Usage: $0 username"
                  exit 1
             fi

             # Remove cron jobs.
             crontab -r -u $1

             # Remove at jobs.
             # Note that it will remove any jobs owned by the same UID,
             # even if it was shared by a different username.
             AT_SPOOL_DIR=/var/spool/cron/atjobs
             find $AT_SPOOL_DIR -name "[^.]*" -type f -user $1 -delete \;

             # Remove print jobs.
             lprm $1

             # All done.
             exit 0


     1mUSERGROUPS_ENAB 22m(boolean)
         If set to 4myes24m, 1muserdel 22mwill remove the user's group if it contains  no  more  members,  and
         1museradd 22mwill create by default a group with the name of the user.

1mFILES0m
     /etc/group
         Group account information.

     /etc/login.defs
         Shadow password suite configuration.

     /etc/passwd
         User account information.

     /etc/shadow
         Secure user account information.

     /etc/shadow-maint/userdel-pre.d/*, /etc/shadow-maint/userdel-post.d/*
         Run-part  files  to  execute  during user deletion. The environment variable 1mACTION 22mwill be
         populated with 1muserdel 22mand 1mSUBJECT 22mwith the username.  userdel-pre.d will be executed prior
         to any user deletion.  userdel-post.d will execute after user deletion. If a  script  exits
         non-zero then execution will terminate.

     /etc/subgid
         Per user subordinate group IDs.

     /etc/subuid
         Per user subordinate user IDs.

1mEXIT VALUES0m
     The 1muserdel 22mcommand exits with the following values:

     4m00m
         success

     4m10m
         can't update password file

     4m20m
         invalid command syntax

     4m60m
         specified user doesn't exist

     4m80m
         user currently logged in

     4m100m
         can't update group file

     4m120m
         can't remove home directory

1mCAVEATS0m
     1muserdel  22mwill not allow you to remove an account if there are running processes which belong to
     this account. In that case, you may have to kill those processes or lock the user's password or
     account and remove the account later. The 1m-f 22moption can force the deletion of this account.

     You should manually check all file systems to ensure that no files remain owned by this user.

     You may not remove any NIS attributes on a NIS client.  This  must  be  performed  on  the  NIS
     server.

     If 1mUSERGROUPS_ENAB 22mis defined to 4myes24m in /etc/login.defs, 1muserdel 22mwill delete the group with the
     same name as the user. To avoid inconsistencies in the passwd and group databases, 1muserdel 22mwill
     check that this group is not used as a primary group for another user, and will just warn with‐
     out deleting the group otherwise. The 1m-f 22moption can force the deletion of this group.

1mSEE ALSO0m
     1mchfn22m(1),  1mchsh22m(1), 1mpasswd22m(1), 1mlogin.defs22m(5), 1mgpasswd22m(8), 1mgroupadd22m(8), 1mgroupdel22m(8), 1mgroupmod22m(8),
     1msubgid22m(5), 1msubuid22m(5), 1museradd22m(8), 1musermod22m(8).

vendstat.text:
========
vendstat
========

------------------------------------------
query InfiniBand vendor specific functions
------------------------------------------

:Date: 2017-08-21
:Manual section: 8
:Manual group: Open IB Diagnostics

SYNOPSIS
========

vendstat [options] <lid|guid>

DESCRIPTION
===========

vendstat uses vendor specific MADs to access beyond the IB spec
vendor specific functionality. Currently, there is support for
Mellanox InfiniSwitch-III (IS3) and InfiniSwitch-IV (IS4).

OPTIONS
=======

**-N**
	show IS3 or IS4 general information.

**-w**
	show IS3 port xmit wait counters.

**-i**
	show IS4 counter group info.

**-c <num,num>**
	configure IS4 counter groups.

	Configure IS4 counter groups 0 and 1. Such configuration is not
	persistent across IS4 reboot.  First number is for counter group 0 and
	second is for counter group 1.

	Group 0 counter config values:

::

		0 - PortXmitDataSL0-7
		1 - PortXmitDataSL8-15
		2 - PortRcvDataSL0-7

	Group 1 counter config values:

::

		1 - PortXmitDataSL8-15
		2 - PortRcvDataSL0-7
		8 - PortRcvDataSL8-15

**-R, --Read <addr,mask>**
	Read configuration space record at addr

**-W, --Write <addr,val,mask>**
	Write configuration space record at addr


Addressing Flags
----------------

.. Define the common option -G

**-G, --Guid**     The address specified is a Port GUID


.. Define the common option -L

**-L, --Lid**   The address specified is a LID


.. Define the common option -s

**-s, --sm_port <smlid>**     use 'smlid' as the target lid for SA queries.


Port Selection flags
--------------------

.. Define the common option -C

**-C, --Ca <ca_name>**    use the specified ca_name.


.. Define the common option -P

**-P, --Port <ca_port>**    use the specified ca_port.


.. Define the common option -Y

**-Y, --pkey-idx <idx>**
  P_Key table index (0-65535, default 0) used for the outgoing SA/GMP MADs.
  SMP (SMI directed-route/LID-routed) MADs always use P_Key index 0.

.. Explanation of local port selection

Local port Selection
--------------------

Multiple port/Multiple CA support: when no IB device or port is specified
(see the "local umad parameters" below), the libibumad library
selects the port to use by the following criteria:

	1. the first port that is ACTIVE.
	2. if not found, the first port that is UP (physical link up).

	If a port and/or CA name is specified, the libibumad library attempts
	to fulfill the user request, and will fail if it is not possible.

	For example:

        ::

	    ibaddr                 # use the first port (criteria #1 above)
	    ibaddr -C mthca1       # pick the best port from "mthca1" only.
	    ibaddr -P 2            # use the second (active/up) port from the first available IB device.
	    ibaddr -C mthca0 -P 2  # use the specified port only.


Debugging flags
---------------

.. Define the common option -d

-d
        raise the IB debugging level.
        May be used several times (-ddd or -d -d -d).


.. Define the common option -e

-e      show send and receive errors (timeouts and others)

.. Define the common option -h

**-h, --help**      show the usage message


.. Define the common option -v

**-v, --verbose**
        increase the application verbosity level.
        May be used several times (-vv or -v -v -v)


.. Define the common option -V

**-V, --version**     show the version info.


Configuration flags
-------------------

.. Define the common option -t

**-t, --timeout <timeout_ms>** override the default timeout for the solicited mads.


.. Define the common option -z

**--config, -z  <config_file>** Specify alternate config file.

        Default: @IBDIAG_CONFIG_PATH@/ibdiag.conf


FILES
=====

.. Common text for the config file

CONFIG FILE
-----------

@IBDIAG_CONFIG_PATH@/ibdiag.conf

A global config file is provided to set some of the common options for all
tools.  See supplied config file for details.


EXAMPLES
========

::

	vendstat -N 6		# read IS3 or IS4 general information
	vendstat -w 6		# read IS3 port xmit wait counters
	vendstat -i 6 12	# read IS4 port 12 counter group info
	vendstat -c 0,1 6 12	# configure IS4 port 12 counter groups for PortXmitDataSL
	vendstat -c 2,8 6 12	# configure IS4 port 12 counter groups for PortRcvDataSL

AUTHOR
======

Hal Rosenstock
	< hal.rosenstock@gmail.com >

wipefs.text:
4mWIPEFS24m(8)                               System Administration                              4mWIPEFS24m(8)

1mNAME0m
     wipefs - wipe a signature from a device

1mSYNOPSIS0m
     1mwipefs 22m[options] 4mdevice24m...

     1mwipefs 22m[1m--backup22m] 1m-o 4m22moffset24m 4mdevice24m...

     1mwipefs 22m[1m--backup22m] 1m-a 4m22mdevice24m...

1mDESCRIPTION0m
     1mwipefs 22mcan erase filesystem, raid or partition-table signatures (magic strings) from the speci‐
     fied 4mdevice24m to make the signatures invisible for libblkid. 1mwipefs 22mdoes not erase the filesystem
     itself nor any other data from the device.

     When  used  without  any options, 1mwipefs 22mlists all visible filesystems and the offsets of their
     basic signatures. The default output is subject to change. So  whenever  possible,  you  should
     avoid using default outputs in your scripts. Always explicitly define expected columns by using
     1m--output 4m22mcolumns-list24m in environments where a stable output is required.

     1mwipefs  22mcalls  the 1mBLKRRPART 22mioctl when it has erased a partition-table signature to inform the
     kernel about the change. The ioctl is called as the last step and when all specified signatures
     from all specified devices are already erased. This feature can be used to wipe content on par‐
     tition devices as well as a partition table  on  a  disk  device,  for  example  by  1mwipefs  -a0m
     1m/dev/sdc1 /dev/sdc2 /dev/sdc22m.

     Note  that  some  filesystems  and some partition tables store more magic strings on the device
     (e.g., FAT, ZFS, GPT). The 1mwipefs 22mcommand (since v2.31)  lists  all  the  offsets  where  magic
     strings have been detected.

     When  option 1m-a 22mis used, all magic strings that are visible for 1mlibblkid22m(3) are erased. In this
     case the 1mwipefs 22mscans the device again after each modification (erase) until no magic string is
     found.

     Note that by default 1mwipefs 22mdoes not erase nested partition tables on non-whole  disk  devices.
     For this the option 1m--force 22mis required.

1mOPTIONS0m
     1m-a22m, 1m--all0m
         Erase  all available signatures. The set of erased signatures can be restricted with the 1m-t0m
         option. When performed on a partitioned whole-disk device like /dev/sdX, it will erase only
         the partition tables, not the content of the partitions.

     1m-b22m, 1m--backup22m[1m=4m22mdir24m]
         Create a signature backup to the file 4mwipefs-<devname>-<offset>.bak24m in 4m$HOME24m or the  direc‐
         tory specified as the optional argument. For more details see the 1mEXAMPLE 22msection.

     1m-f22m, 1m--force0m
         Force erasure, even if the filesystem is mounted. This is also required in order to erase a
         nested partition-table signature on a non-whole disk device.

     1m-J22m, 1m--json0m
         Use JSON output format.

     1m--lock22m[1m=4m22mmode24m]
         Use  an exclusive BSD lock for the device or file that is operated upon. The optional argu‐
         ment 4mmode24m can be 1myes 22m(1m122m), 1mno 22m(1m022m), or 1mnonblock22m. If the 4mmode24m argument is omitted, it defaults
         to 1myes22m. This option overrides the environment variable 1m$LOCK_BLOCK_DEVICE22m. The  default  is
         to  not  use any lock at all, but using a lock is recommended to avoid collisions with 1msys‐0m
         1mtemd-udevd22m(8) or other tools.

     1m-i22m, 1m--noheadings0m
         Do not print a header line.

     1m-O22m, 1m--output 4m22mlist0m
         Specify which output columns to print. Use 1m--help 22mto get a list of all supported columns.

     1m-n22m, 1m--no-act0m
         Causes everything to be done except for the 1mwrite22m(2) call.

     1m-o22m, 1m--offset 4m22moffset0m
         Specify the location (in bytes) of the signature which should be erased  from  the  device.
         The  4moffset24m  number may include a "0x" prefix; then the number will be interpreted as a hex
         value. It is possible to specify multiple 1m-o 22moptions.

         The 4moffset24m argument may be  followed  by  the  multiplicative  suffixes  KiB  (=1024),  MiB
         (=1024*1024),  and  so  on for GiB, TiB, PiB, EiB, ZiB and YiB (the "iB" is optional, e.g.,
         "K" has the same meaning as "KiB"), or the suffixes KB (=1000), MB (=1000*1000), and so  on
         for GB, TB, PB, EB, ZB and YB.

     1m-p22m, 1m--parsable0m
         Print out in parsable instead of printable format. Encode all potentially unsafe characters
         of a string to the corresponding hex value prefixed by '\x'.

     1m-q22m, 1m--quiet0m
         Suppress any messages after a successful signature wipe.

     1m-t22m, 1m--types 4m22mlist0m
         Limit  the  set  of  printed or erased signatures. More than one type may be specified in a
         comma-separated list. The list or individual types can be prefixed with 'no' to specify the
         types on which no action should be taken. For more details see 1mmount22m(8).

     1m-h22m, 1m--help0m
         Display help text and exit.

     1m-V22m, 1m--version0m
         Display version and exit.

1mENVIRONMENT0m
     LIBBLKID_DEBUG=all
         enables 1mlibblkid22m(3) debug output.

     LOCK_BLOCK_DEVICE=<mode>
         use exclusive BSD lock. The mode is "1" or "0". See 1m--lock 22mfor more details.

     1mLIBSMARTCOLS_DEBUG22m=all
         enables libsmartcols debug output.

     1mLIBSMARTCOLS_DEBUG_PADDING22m=on
         use visible padding characters.

     1mLIBSMARTCOLS_JSON22m=compact|lines
         Controls JSON output format when using 1m--json22m. Supported values are 1mcompact 22mfor JSON output
         with minimal whitespace, and 1mlines 22mfor JSON Lines format (one JSON object per line). If un‐
         set or set to any other value, pretty-printed JSON is used.

1mEXAMPLES0m
     1mwipefs /dev/sda22m*
         Prints information about sda and all partitions on sda.

     1mwipefs --all --backup /dev/sdb0m
         Erases all signatures from  the  device  4m/dev/sdb24m  and  creates  a  signature  backup  file
         4m~/wipefs-sdb-<offset>.bak24m for each signature.

     1mdd if=~/wipefs-sdb-0x00000438.bak of=/dev/sdb seek=$((0x00000438)) bs=1 conv=notrunc0m
         Restores an ext2 signature from the backup file 4m~/wipefs-sdb-0x00000438.bak24m.

1mAUTHORS0m
     34mKarel Zak 0m<kzak@redhat.com>

1mSEE ALSO0m
     1mblkid22m(8), 1mfindfs22m(8)

1mREPORTING BUGS0m
     For bug reports, use the 34missue tracker 0m<https://github.com/util-linux/util-linux/issues>.

1mAVAILABILITY0m
     The  1mwipefs 22mcommand is part of the util-linux package which can be downloaded from 34mLinux Kernel0m
     34mArchive 0m<https://www.kernel.org/pub/linux/utils/util-linux/>.

xz.text:
4mXZ24m(1)                                         XZ Utils                                         4mXZ24m(1)

1mNAME0m
     xz, unxz, xzcat, lzma, unlzma, lzcat - Compress or decompress .xz and .lzma files

1mSYNOPSIS0m
     1mxz 22m[4moption...24m]  [4mfile...24m]

1mCOMMAND ALIASES0m
     1munxz 22mis equivalent to 1mxz --decompress22m.
     1mxzcat 22mis equivalent to 1mxz --decompress --stdout22m.
     1mlzma 22mis equivalent to 1mxz --format=lzma22m.
     1munlzma 22mis equivalent to 1mxz --format=lzma --decompress22m.
     1mlzcat 22mis equivalent to 1mxz --format=lzma --decompress --stdout22m.

     When writing scripts that need to decompress files, it is recommended to always use the name 1mxz0m
     with appropriate arguments (1mxz -d 22mor 1mxz -dc22m) instead of the names 1munxz 22mand 1mxzcat22m.

1mDESCRIPTION0m
     1mxz  22mis  a general-purpose data compression tool with command line syntax similar to 1mgzip22m(1) and
     1mbzip222m(1).  The native file format is the 1m.xz 22mformat, but the legacy 1m.lzma 22mformat used  by  LZMA
     Utils and raw compressed streams with no container format headers are also supported.  In addi‐
     tion, decompression of the 1m.lz 22mformat used by 1mlzip 22mis supported.

     1mxz  22mcompresses or decompresses each 4mfile24m according to the selected operation mode.  If no 4mfiles0m
     are given or 4mfile24m is 1m-22m, 1mxz 22mreads from standard input and writes the processed data to  standard
     output.   1mxz 22mwill refuse (display an error and skip the 4mfile24m) to write compressed data to stan‐
     dard output if it is a terminal.  Similarly, 1mxz 22mwill refuse to read compressed data from  stan‐
     dard input if it is a terminal.

     Unless  1m--stdout  22mis  specified, 4mfiles24m other than 1m- 22mare written to a new file whose name is de‐
     rived from the source 4mfile24m name:

     •  When compressing, the suffix of the target file format (1m.xz 22mor 1m.lzma22m)  is  appended  to  the
        source filename to get the target filename.

     •  When  decompressing,  the  1m.xz22m, 1m.lzma22m, or 1m.lz 22msuffix is removed from the filename to get the
        target filename.  1mxz 22malso recognizes the suffixes 1m.txz 22mand 1m.tlz22m, and replaces them with  the
        1m.tar 22msuffix.

     If the target file already exists, an error is displayed and the 4mfile24m is skipped.

     Unless  writing  to  standard output, 1mxz 22mwill display a warning and skip the 4mfile24m if any of the
     following applies:

     •  4mFile24m is not a regular file.  Symbolic links are not followed, and thus they are not  consid‐
        ered to be regular files.

     •  4mFile24m has more than one hard link.

     •  4mFile24m has setuid, setgid, or sticky bit set.

     •  The  operation  mode is set to compress and the 4mfile24m already has a suffix of the target file
        format (1m.xz 22mor 1m.txz 22mwhen compressing to the 1m.xz 22mformat, and 1m.lzma 22mor 1m.tlz  22mwhen  compressing
        to the 1m.lzma 22mformat).

     •  The  operation  mode  is  set to decompress and the 4mfile24m doesn't have a suffix of any of the
        supported file formats (1m.xz22m, 1m.txz22m, 1m.lzma22m, 1m.tlz22m, or 1m.lz22m).

     After successfully compressing or decompressing the 4mfile24m, 1mxz 22mcopies the owner,  group,  permis‐
     sions,  access time, and modification time from the source 4mfile24m to the target file.  If copying
     the group fails, the permissions are modified so that the target file doesn't become accessible
     to users who didn't have permission to access the source  4mfile24m.   1mxz  22mdoesn't  support  copying
     other metadata like access control lists or extended attributes yet.

     Once the target file has been successfully closed, the source 4mfile24m is removed unless 1m--keep 22mwas
     specified.   The source 4mfile24m is never removed if the output is written to standard output or if
     an error occurs.

     Sending 1mSIGINFO 22mor 1mSIGUSR1 22mto the 1mxz 22mprocess makes it print progress  information  to  standard
     error.  This has only limited use since when standard error is a terminal, using 1m--verbose 22mwill
     display an automatically updating progress indicator.

   1mMemory usage0m
     The  memory  usage  of 1mxz 22mvaries from a few hundred kilobytes to several gigabytes depending on
     the compression settings.  The settings used when compressing a file determine the  memory  re‐
     quirements  of the decompressor.  Typically the decompressor needs 5 % to 20 % of the amount of
     memory that the compressor needed when creating the file.  For example,  decompressing  a  file
     created  with  1mxz  -9  22mcurrently  requires 65 MiB of memory.  Still, it is possible to have 1m.xz0m
     files that require several gigabytes of memory to decompress.

     Especially users of older systems may find the possibility of very large memory usage annoying.
     To prevent uncomfortable surprises, 1mxz 22mhas a built-in memory usage limiter, which  is  disabled
     by  default.  While some operating systems provide ways to limit the memory usage of processes,
     relying on it wasn't deemed to be flexible enough (for example, using 1mulimit22m(1) to  limit  vir‐
     tual memory tends to cripple 1mmmap22m(2)).

     The  memory  usage limiter can be enabled with the command line option 1m--memlimit=4m22mlimit24m.  Often
     it is more convenient to enable the limiter by default  by  setting  the  environment  variable
     1mXZ_DEFAULTS22m, for example, 1mXZ_DEFAULTS=--memlimit=150MiB22m.  It is possible to set the limits sep‐
     arately for compression and decompression by using 1m--memlimit-compress=4m22mlimit24m and 1m--memlimit-de‐0m
     1mcompress=4m22mlimit24m.   Using these two options outside 1mXZ_DEFAULTS 22mis rarely useful because a single
     run of 1mxz 22mcannot do both compression and decompression and 1m--memlimit=4m22mlimit24m (or  1m-M  4m22mlimit24m)  is
     shorter to type on the command line.

     If  the  specified  memory usage limit is exceeded when decompressing, 1mxz 22mwill display an error
     and decompressing the file will fail.  If the limit is exceeded when compressing, 1mxz  22mwill  try
     to  scale  the  settings down so that the limit is no longer exceeded (except when using 1m--for‐0m
     1mmat=raw 22mor 1m--no-adjust22m).  This way the operation won't fail unless the  limit  is  very  small.
     The  scaling  of  the settings is done in steps that don't match the compression level presets,
     for example, if the limit is only slightly less than the amount required for 1mxz  -922m,  the  set‐
     tings will be scaled down only a little, not all the way down to 1mxz -822m.

   1mConcatenation and padding with .xz files0m
     It is possible to concatenate 1m.xz 22mfiles as is.  1mxz 22mwill decompress such files as if they were a
     single 1m.xz 22mfile.

     It  is  possible  to insert padding between the concatenated parts or after the last part.  The
     padding must consist of null bytes and the size of the padding  must  be  a  multiple  of  four
     bytes.   This  can  be useful, for example, if the 1m.xz 22mfile is stored on a medium that measures
     file sizes in 512-byte blocks.

     Concatenation and padding are not allowed with 1m.lzma 22mfiles or raw streams.

1mOPTIONS0m
   1mInteger suffixes and special values0m
     In most places where an integer argument is expected, an optional suffix is supported to easily
     indicate large integers.  There must be no space between the integer and the suffix.

     1mKiB    22mMultiply the integer by 1,024 (2^10).  1mKi22m, 1mk22m, 1mkB22m, 1mK22m, and 1mKB 22mare accepted as synonyms for
            1mKiB22m.

     1mMiB    22mMultiply the integer by 1,048,576 (2^20).  1mMi22m, 1mm22m, 1mM22m, and 1mMB 22mare accepted as synonyms for
            1mMiB22m.

     1mGiB    22mMultiply the integer by 1,073,741,824 (2^30).  1mGi22m, 1mg22m, 1mG22m, and 1mGB 22mare accepted as synonyms
            for 1mGiB22m.

     The special value 1mmax 22mcan be used to indicate the maximum integer value supported  by  the  op‐
     tion.

   1mOperation mode0m
     If multiple operation mode options are given, the last one takes effect.

     1m-z22m, 1m--compress0m
            Compress.  This is the default operation mode when no operation mode option is specified
            and  no other operation mode is implied from the command name (for example, 1munxz 22mimplies
            1m--decompress22m).

            After successful compression, the source file is removed unless writing to standard out‐
            put or 1m--keep 22mwas specified.

     1m-d22m, 1m--decompress22m, 1m--uncompress0m
            Decompress.  After successful decompression, the source file is removed  unless  writing
            to standard output or 1m--keep 22mwas specified.

     1m-t22m, 1m--test0m
            Test  the  integrity  of  compressed  4mfiles24m.   This option is equivalent to 1m--decompress0m
            1m--stdout 22mexcept that the decompressed data is discarded  instead  of  being  written  to
            standard output.  No files are created or removed.

     1m-l22m, 1m--list0m
            Print  information  about  compressed 4mfiles24m.  No uncompressed output is produced, and no
            files are created or removed.  In list mode, the program cannot read the compressed data
            from standard input or from other unseekable sources.

            The default listing shows basic information about 4mfiles24m, one file per line.  To get more
            detailed information, use also the 1m--verbose 22moption.  For  even  more  information,  use
            1m--verbose  22mtwice, but note that this may be slow, because getting all the extra informa‐
            tion requires many seeks.  The width of verbose output exceeds 80 characters, so  piping
            the output to, for example, 1mless -S 22mmay be convenient if the terminal isn't wide enough.

            The  exact output may vary between 1mxz 22mversions and different locales.  For machine-read‐
            able output, 1m--robot --list 22mshould be used.

   1mOperation modifiers0m
     1m-k22m, 1m--keep0m
            Don't delete the input files.

            Since 1mxz 22m5.2.6, this option also makes 1mxz 22mcompress or decompress even if the input is  a
            symbolic link to a regular file, has more than one hard link, or has the setuid, setgid,
            or  sticky  bit  set.   The setuid, setgid, and sticky bits are not copied to the target
            file.  In earlier versions this was only done with 1m--force22m.

     1m-f22m, 1m--force0m
            This option has several effects:

            •  If the target file already exists, delete it before compressing or decompressing.

            •  Compress or decompress even if the input is a symbolic link to a  regular  file,  has
               more  than  one hard link, or has the setuid, setgid, or sticky bit set.  The setuid,
               setgid, and sticky bits are not copied to the target file.

            •  When used with 1m--decompress --stdout 22mand 1mxz 22mcannot recognize the type of  the  source
               file, copy the source file as is to standard output.  This allows 1mxzcat --force 22mto be
               used  like  1mcat22m(1) for files that have not been compressed with 1mxz22m.  Note that in fu‐
               ture, 1mxz 22mmight support new compressed file formats, which may make 1mxz 22mdecompress more
               types of files instead of copying them as is to standard output.  1m--format=4m22mformat24m can
               be used to restrict 1mxz 22mto decompress only a single file format.

     1m-c22m, 1m--stdout22m, 1m--to-stdout0m
            Write the compressed or decompressed data to standard output instead of  a  file.   This
            implies 1m--keep22m.

     1m--single-stream0m
            Decompress  only the first 1m.xz 22mstream, and silently ignore possible remaining input data
            following the stream.  Normally such trailing garbage makes 1mxz 22mdisplay an error.

            1mxz 22mnever decompresses more than one stream from 1m.lzma 22mfiles or raw streams, but this op‐
            tion still makes 1mxz 22mignore the possible trailing  data  after  the  1m.lzma  22mfile  or  raw
            stream.

            This option has no effect if the operation mode is not 1m--decompress 22mor 1m--test22m.

            Since 1mxz 22m5.7.1alpha, 1m--single-stream 22mimplies 1m--keep22m.

     1m--no-sparse0m
            Disable  creation of sparse files.  By default, if decompressing into a regular file, 1mxz0m
            tries to make the file sparse if the decompressed data contains long sequences of binary
            zeros.  It also works when writing to standard output as long as standard output is con‐
            nected to a regular file and certain additional conditions are  met  to  make  it  safe.
            Creating sparse files may save disk space and speed up the decompression by reducing the
            amount of disk I/O.

     1m-S 4m22m.suf24m, 1m--suffix=4m22m.suf0m
            When  compressing,  use  4m.suf24m as the suffix for the target file instead of 1m.xz 22mor 1m.lzma22m.
            If not writing to standard output and the source file already has  the  suffix  4m.suf24m,  a
            warning is displayed and the file is skipped.

            When  decompressing,  recognize files with the suffix 4m.suf24m in addition to files with the
            1m.xz22m, 1m.txz22m, 1m.lzma22m, 1m.tlz22m, or 1m.lz 22msuffix.  If the source file has the suffix 4m.suf24m, the suf‐
            fix is removed to get the target filename.

            When compressing or decompressing raw streams (1m--format=raw22m), the suffix must always  be
            specified  unless writing to standard output, because there is no default suffix for raw
            streams.

     1m--files22m[1m=4m22mfile24m]
            Read the filenames to process from 4mfile24m; if 4mfile24m is omitted,  filenames  are  read  from
            standard input.  Filenames must be terminated with the newline character.  A dash (1m-22m) is
            taken  as  a  regular  filename; it doesn't mean standard input.  If filenames are given
            also as command line arguments, they are processed before the filenames read from 4mfile24m.

     1m--files022m[1m=4m22mfile24m]
            This is identical to 1m--files22m[1m=4m22mfile24m] except that each filename must  be  terminated  with
            the null character.

   1mBasic file format and compression options0m
     1m-F 4m22mformat24m, 1m--format=4m22mformat0m
            Specify the file 4mformat24m to compress or decompress:

            1mauto   22mThis  is  the  default.  When compressing, 1mauto 22mis equivalent to 1mxz22m.  When decom‐
                   pressing, the format of the input file is automatically detected.  Note that  raw
                   streams (created with 1m--format=raw22m) cannot be auto-detected.

            1mxz     22mCompress to the 1m.xz 22mfile format, or accept only 1m.xz 22mfiles when decompressing.

            1mlzma22m, 1malone0m
                   Compress  to the legacy 1m.lzma 22mfile format, or accept only 1m.lzma 22mfiles when decom‐
                   pressing.  The alternative name 1malone 22mis  provided  for  backwards  compatibility
                   with LZMA Utils.

            1mlzip   22mAccept only 1m.lz 22mfiles when decompressing.  Compression is not supported.

                   The  1m.lz 22mformat versions 0 and 1 are supported.  Version 0 files were produced by
                   1mlzip 22m1.3 and older.  Such files aren't common but may be found from file archives
                   as a few source packages were released in this format.   People  might  have  old
                   personal  files in this format too.  Decompression support for the format version
                   0 was removed in 1mlzip 22m1.18.  1mlzip 22m1.4 and later create files in the  format  ver‐
                   sion 1.

            1mraw    22mCompress  or  uncompress  a  raw stream (no headers).  This is meant for advanced
                   users only.  To decode raw streams, you  need  use  1m--format=raw  22mand  explicitly
                   specify  the filter chain, which normally would have been stored in the container
                   headers.

     1m-C 4m22mcheck24m, 1m--check=4m22mcheck0m
            Specify the type of the integrity check.  The check is calculated from the  uncompressed
            data  and  stored in the 1m.xz 22mfile.  This option has an effect only when compressing into
            the 1m.xz 22mformat; the 1m.lzma 22mformat doesn't support integrity checks.  The integrity  check
            (if any) is verified when the 1m.xz 22mfile is decompressed.

            Supported 4mcheck24m types:

            1mnone   22mDon't calculate an integrity check at all.  This is usually a bad idea.  This can
                   be useful when integrity of the data is verified by other means anyway.

            1mcrc32  22mCalculate CRC32 using the polynomial from IEEE-802.3 (Ethernet).

            1mcrc64  22mCalculate  CRC64  using the polynomial from ECMA-182.  This is the default, since
                   it is slightly better than CRC32 at detecting damaged files and the speed differ‐
                   ence is negligible.

            1msha2560m
                   Calculate SHA-256.  This is somewhat slower than CRC32 and CRC64.

            Integrity of the 1m.xz 22mheaders is always verified with  CRC32.   It  is  not  possible  to
            change or disable it.

     1m--ignore-check0m
            Don't  verify  the integrity check of the compressed data when decompressing.  The CRC32
            values in the 1m.xz 22mheaders will still be verified normally.

            1mDo not use this option unless you know what you are doing.  22mPossible reasons to use this
            option:

            •  Trying to recover data from a corrupt .xz file.

            •  Speeding up decompression.  This matters mostly with SHA-256 or with files that  have
               compressed  extremely well.  It's recommended to not use this option for this purpose
               unless the file integrity is verified externally in some other way.

     1m-0 22m... 1m-90m
            Select a compression preset level.  The default is 1m-622m.  If multiple  preset  levels  are
            specified,  the  last one takes effect.  If a custom filter chain was already specified,

            The selected compression settings determine the memory requirements of the decompressor,

            old  system  with  little RAM.  Specifically, 1mit's not a good idea to blindly use -9 for0m
            1meverything 22mlike it often is with 1mgzip22m(1) and 1mbzip222m(1).

            blocks are compressed independently from each other, which  helps  with  multi-threading
            and  makes  limited random-access decompression possible.  This option is typically used
            to override the default block size in multi-threaded mode, but this option can  be  used
            in single-threaded mode too.

            buffering  input  and output.  The default 4msize24m is three times the LZMA2 dictionary size
            or 1 MiB, whichever is more.  Typically a good value is 2–4 times the size of the  LZMA2
            dictionary  or  at least 1 MiB.  Using 4msize24m less than the LZMA2 dictionary size is waste

            threaded  mode,  the sizes of the blocks are stored in the block headers.  This size in‐

            •  The filter chain specified by 1m--filters2 22mand 4 MiB input

            •  The filter chain specified by 1m--filters2 22mand 4 MiB input

   1mCustom compressor filter chains0m
     A  custom  filter chain allows specifying the compression settings in detail instead of relying
     on the settings associated to the presets.  When a custom filter chain is specified, preset op‐
     tions (1m-0 22m... 1m-9 22mand 1m--extreme22m) earlier on the command line are forgotten.  If a preset  option
     is specified after one or more custom filter chain options, the new preset takes effect and the
     custom filter chain options specified earlier are forgotten.

     A filter chain is comparable to piping on the command line.  When compressing, the uncompressed
     input  goes  to the first filter, whose output goes to the next filter (if any).  The output of
     the last filter gets written to the compressed file.  The maximum  number  of  filters  in  the
     chain is four, but typically a filter chain has only one or two filters.

     Many  filters  have limitations on where they can be in the filter chain: some filters can work
     only as the last filter in the chain, some only as a non-last filter, and some work in any  po‐
     sition in the chain.  Depending on the filter, this limitation is either inherent to the filter
     design or exists to prevent security issues.

     A  custom  filter  chain can be specified in two different ways.  The options 1m--filters=4m22mfilters0m
     and 1m--filters1=4m22mfilters24m ... 1m--filters9=4m22mfilters24m allow specifying an entire filter  chain  in  one
     option  using the liblzma filter string syntax.  Alternatively, a filter chain can be specified
     by using one or more individual filter options in the order  they  are  wanted  in  the  filter
     chain.   That is, the order of the individual filter options is significant!  When decoding raw
     streams (1m--format=raw22m), the filter chain must be specified in the same order as it  was  speci‐
     fied when compressing.  Any individual filter or preset options specified before the full chain
     option  (1m--filters=4m22mfilters24m)  will  be  forgotten.   Individual filters specified after the full
     chain option will reset the filter chain.

     Both the full and individual filter options take filter-specific 4moptions24m as  a  comma-separated
     list.  Extra commas in 4moptions24m are ignored.  Every option has a default value, so specify those
     you want to change.

     To  see  the  whole  filter chain and 4moptions24m, use 1mxz -vv 22m(that is, use 1m--verbose 22mtwice).  This
     works also for viewing the filter chain options used by presets.

            rated  by spaces or two dashes (1m--22m).  4mfilters24m may need to be quoted on the shell command

            be prefixed with a 1m- 22mand followed with zero or more flags.  The only supported flag is 1me0m

            last filter in the chain.

            format,  which  supports  only  LZMA1.  LZMA2 is an updated version of LZMA1 to fix some
            practical issues of LZMA1.  The 1m.xz 22mformat uses LZMA2 and doesn't support LZMA1 at  all.
            Compression speed and ratios of LZMA1 and LZMA2 are practically the same.

            LZMA1 and LZMA2 share the same set of 4moptions24m:

            1mpreset=4m22mpreset0m

                   currently 1me22m, which matches 1m--extreme22m.  If no 1mpreset  22mis  specified,  the  default

                   processed uncompressed data is kept in memory.  The algorithm tries to  find  re‐
                   peating  byte sequences (matches) in the uncompressed data, and replace them with
                   references to the data currently in the dictionary.  The bigger  the  dictionary,
                   the  higher is the chance to find a match.  Thus, increasing dictionary 4msize24m usu‐
                   ally improves compression ratio, but a dictionary bigger  than  the  uncompressed
                   file is waste of memory.

                   Typical  dictionary  4msize24m  is  from 64 KiB to 64 MiB.  The minimum is 4 KiB.  The
                   maximum for compression is currently 1.5 GiB (1536 MiB).   The  decompressor  al‐
                   ready  supports dictionaries up to one byte less than 4 GiB, which is the maximum
                   for the LZMA1 and LZMA2 stream formats.

                   Dictionary 4msize24m and match finder (4mmf24m) together determine the memory usage of  the
                   LZMA1 or LZMA2 encoder.  The same (or bigger) dictionary 4msize24m is required for de‐
                   compressing  that was used when compressing, thus the memory usage of the decoder
                   is determined by the dictionary size used  when  compressing.   The  1m.xz  22mheaders
                   store  the  dictionary  4msize24m  either  as 2^4mn24m or 2^4mn24m + 2^(4mn24m-1), so these 4msizes24m are
